topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Step-by-Step Instructions
topics.description: Step-by-step instructions for everyday tasks (making a sandwich, brushing teeth); that if instructions are wrong or missing, things go wrong; computers follow instructions exactly
evidence: Write or describe step-by-step instructions for a simple everyday task
Predict what goes wrong if a step is missing or in the wrong order
Explain that a computer follows instructions exactly — it cannot guess what you meant
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had to write instructions for making a jam sandwich so precise that even a robot could follow them, could they include every single step?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Decisions and repeats in algorithms
topics.description: Follow and describe algorithms that include a sequence of steps, branching (a decision such as 'if it is raining, take an umbrella') and iteration (repeating steps, such as 'hop 3 times')
evidence: Follow movement instructions that include a repeat (e.g. 'repeat 3 times: step forward, clap') and describe which part was repeated
Follow an algorithm with a decision (e.g. 'If the card is red, put it in the box; otherwise put it on the table') and explain what the decision did
Describe the steps, decision and repeat in a familiar routine, such as getting ready for school
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a game like 'If I clap, jump; if I stomp, sit — repeat 5 times', can {{name}} follow the rules and explain the 'if' part and the 'repeat' part?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Decisions and input in programs
topics.description: Use input (key presses, mouse clicks, sensors or typed answers) and branching blocks (if ... then, if ... then ... else) with comparison operators to make a visual program respond to the user
evidence: Program a character to move left and right when the arrow keys are pressed
Write a quiz question that asks for an answer and uses 'if answer = 12 then say Correct, else say Try again'
Use a comparison such as 'if score > 5' or 'if touching colour red' to change what the program does and explain the condition
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} make a simple game in a coding app where pressing the arrow keys moves a character, or a quiz that says 'Correct' or 'Try again'?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Loops in programs
topics.description: Use repeat (loop) blocks in a visual program to repeat actions a set number of times or forever, and identify where a loop makes a program shorter
evidence: Rewrite a program that repeats 'move 10 steps' four times so that it uses one repeat block
Use a repeat block to draw a square with a sprite or robot (repeat 4: move, turn 90 degrees)
Explain the difference between 'repeat 10' and 'forever' blocks with an example of when to use each
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a coding app, can {{name}} use a 'repeat' block to make a character draw a square or dance — instead of dragging the same blocks over and over?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: My first visual program
topics.description: Implement a simple algorithm as a visual (block-based) program — a start event, a sequence of blocks, run and observe — in an environment such as Scratch, ScratchJr or a programmable robot app
evidence: Drag blocks into a sequence so a character moves, speaks and changes costume when the green flag is clicked
Run the program and check that it does what the planned algorithm said
Swap two blocks and explain how the order of blocks changes what the program does
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} used a block-coding app like Scratch to make a character move and talk — and can they explain what happens if they swap the order of the blocks?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Testing and debugging programs
topics.description: Test visual programs by predicting what should happen, running them, finding where the behaviour differs (bugs) and fixing them one change at a time
evidence: Predict what a short program will do, run it and compare the result with the prediction
Find and fix a bug in a given program (e.g. a character that turns the wrong way or a loop that repeats too many times)
Explain how they tracked down the bug (e.g. running one part at a time, checking each block against the algorithm)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}}'s coding project doesn't work the way they wanted, do they test it, hunt for the 'bug' and fix it step by step rather than starting over?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Building and testing programs
topics.description: Implement a designed algorithm as a visual program combining control structures (sequence, multiple branches with if ... else, repeat until), variables and user input, and test it with planned test cases, refining it until it works for all of them
evidence: Implement their own algorithm (e.g. a quiz, game or sorting tool) as a visual program using if ... else branches, a 'repeat until' loop, a variable and user input
Write and run test cases with expected results, including unusual inputs (e.g. a wrong answer, a blank answer, the highest score), and record the outcomes
Refine the program after testing and user feedback and explain what each change fixed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} built a complete game or quiz in a coding app — planning it first, testing it with tricky answers, and improving it until it works properly?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Variables in programs
topics.description: Create and use variables in visual programs to store and change values — such as a score, a timer, a counter or a user's answer — and use them in conditions
evidence: Create a 'score' variable in a game that starts at 0 and increases by 1 each time the player catches an object
Store a user's typed name in a variable and use it in a message (e.g. 'Hello Sam!')
Use a variable in a condition (e.g. 'if lives = 0 then game over') and explain what the variable holds at each stage
topics.assessmentPrompt: In a game {{name}} made with block coding, can they make a score that goes up each time the player wins a point, and end the game when the lives run out?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI in Daily Life
topics.description: Spotting AI in daily life: face unlock on a phone, video recommendations, spelling auto-correct, automatic doors that detect people; technology that seems to 'know' things
evidence: Identify at least five examples of AI in their daily life
Explain that these technologies use patterns and data, not magic or real thinking
Describe one way AI makes their life easier and one time it might not work perfectly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} point out several things they use every day — like auto-correct or face unlock — and explain that these are examples of AI?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Real-World Robots
topics.description: What a robot really is — not the sci-fi version; robots in factories, robot vacuum cleaners, robot arms in surgery; that robots follow instructions given by people
evidence: Describe what a robot is (a machine that follows instructions to do a task)
Name at least three real robots and what they do
Explain that robots are not alive and do not have feelings — they follow instructions people wrote
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw a robot vacuum cleaner, could they explain how it's different from a person cleaning — that it follows instructions rather than thinking for itself?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Smart Versus Not-Smart Devices
topics.description: Sorting objects into 'smart' (can sense and respond) and 'not smart' (just sits there); a toaster vs a smart speaker; introduction to the idea that some machines can sense and respond to the world
evidence: Sort a set of objects into 'smart' (responds to input) and 'not smart' (does the same thing every time)
Explain what makes a smart speaker different from a regular radio
Give an example of a machine that senses something and responds (automatic door, motion-sensor light)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain the difference between a normal light switch and one that turns on automatically when you walk into a room?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Voice Assistants and How They Work
topics.description: What happens when you talk to Alexa, Siri, or Google Assistant; they listen, try to understand, look up answers; sometimes they get it wrong; they are tools, not alive
evidence: Describe the steps that happen when you ask a voice assistant a question (it listens, processes words, finds an answer, speaks back)
Give an example of a time a voice assistant might get something wrong
Explain that a voice assistant is a computer program, not a person — it doesn't understand or feel
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asked Alexa or Siri a question and got a wrong answer, could they explain why the voice assistant sometimes makes mistakes?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Recommendation Systems and Filter Bubbles
topics.description: How recommendation systems work: YouTube, Netflix, and shop websites track what you click and find patterns; filter bubbles; the difference between helpful suggestions and manipulation
evidence: Explain how YouTube or Netflix decides what to suggest next
Describe what a 'filter bubble' is (only seeing things similar to what you already like)
Give one benefit and one risk of recommendation systems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand why YouTube keeps suggesting similar videos to ones they've watched, and could they explain how the recommendation system works?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI in Computer Games
topics.description: How computer game characters 'decide' what to do; simple rule-based AI vs learning AI; NPCs, difficulty adjustment; AI as the opponent in chess or board games
evidence: Explain how a computer opponent in a game decides its moves
Describe the difference between a game character that follows fixed rules and one that learns from the player
Give an example of AI making a game more fun (adjusting difficulty, generating levels)
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} plays a video game against the computer, could they explain how the game's characters 'decide' what to do?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI Mistakes and Limitations
topics.description: Machines make mistakes; they only know what they've been shown; bad training data leads to bad results; AI is not magic — just maths on data; showing edge cases and failures
evidence: Give an example of AI making a mistake (voice assistant mishearing, auto-correct error, wrong recommendation)
Explain that AI mistakes happen because of gaps or errors in training data
Describe why AI is not magic — it follows mathematical rules applied to data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an AI incorrectly identified a picture of a muffin as a chihuahua, could {{name}} explain why that kind of mistake happens?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Humans Versus Machines
topics.description: Comparing human and machine capabilities: creativity, empathy, common sense vs speed, memory, repetition; the Turing Test (simplified); what makes humans unique
evidence: Name at least three things humans are better at than computers (creativity, empathy, common sense)
Name at least three things computers are better at than humans (speed, memory, repetitive tasks)
Describe the Turing Test in simple terms (can a computer fool a person into thinking it's human?)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain what humans are still better at than computers and what computers can do that humans can't?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Machine Learning Basics
topics.description: How machine learning works at a conceptual level: show the computer many examples, it finds patterns, then it makes predictions about new things; hands-on experience with Teachable Machine or similar tool
evidence: Describe the three steps of machine learning in simple terms (give examples, find patterns, make predictions)
Train a simple model using a tool like Teachable Machine and describe what happened
Explain why showing more and better examples makes the model more accurate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} describe how you teach a computer to recognise something — by showing it lots of examples until it spots the pattern?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Patterns and Classification
topics.description: Humans are great at spotting patterns; computers can learn to spot patterns too, but they need lots of examples; sorting and classification activities as the basis of machine learning
evidence: Sort a set of items into categories and explain the rules they used
Explain that computers learn patterns by looking at many examples
Describe why a computer needs more examples than a human to learn the same pattern
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you showed {{name}} pictures of cats and dogs, could they explain how a computer could learn to tell them apart — and why it would need many more pictures than a person would?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI Data Collection and Privacy
topics.description: What data AI systems collect about you; who has it and why it matters; cookies, tracking, smart speakers always listening; your data is valuable
evidence: Name at least three types of personal data that AI systems collect
Explain why personal data is valuable to companies
Describe one step they can take to protect their privacy online
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that apps and websites collect information about what they do online, and could they explain why that matters?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Deepfakes and AI-Generated Content
topics.description: Deepfakes, AI-generated images and text; how to spot them and why they matter; the importance of checking sources; not everything online is real
evidence: Explain what a deepfake is and give an example of AI-generated content
Describe at least two clues that might reveal an image or text was AI-generated
Explain why it matters that AI can create realistic fake content
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw an amazing photo online, would they think to question whether it might have been created by AI rather than captured by a camera?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and Fairness in Decisions
topics.description: Whether AI should make important decisions about people: jobs, loans, justice; who is responsible when AI makes unfair decisions; introduction to algorithmic fairness
evidence: Give an example of an important decision that AI might help make (hiring, medical diagnosis, loan approval)
Explain why letting AI make decisions about people can be risky if the system is biased
Suggest who should be responsible if an AI system makes an unfair decision
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learned that a computer program was deciding who gets a job interview, could they explain why that might be unfair and who should be responsible?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and the Environment
topics.description: AI needs huge amounts of energy and water to train; data centres and their environmental cost; but AI can also help — predicting weather, monitoring deforestation, optimising energy; trade-offs
evidence: Explain that training AI models uses a lot of electricity and water
Give at least two examples of AI being used to help the environment
Describe the trade-off between AI's environmental cost and its environmental benefits
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain that AI needs a lot of energy to work but can also be used to help protect the environment, and discuss whether the trade-off is worth it?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: AI and the Future of Work
topics.description: How AI is changing the world of work: some jobs disappear, new ones are created, many change; jobs AI can't do (yet); what skills matter in an AI world
evidence: Name at least two jobs that AI is changing or replacing and two new jobs AI has created
Explain why creativity, empathy, and problem-solving are skills that matter more in an AI world
Describe how AI might change a specific job they know about (teacher, doctor, farmer) without replacing it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain how AI might change the way people work in the future and which human skills will still be important?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Bias in AI Systems
topics.description: If training data is biased, AI will be biased; examples: facial recognition working better for some skin tones, translation assuming gender; where bias comes from and whether we can fix it
evidence: Explain what bias in AI means using a real-world example
Describe how biased training data leads to biased AI results
Suggest one way to reduce bias in an AI system (use more diverse data, test with different groups)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain why an AI trained mostly on photos of light-skinned faces might not work as well for people with darker skin?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Designing Fair AI Rules
topics.description: Design thinking applied to AI ethics: if you were designing an AI system, what rules would you give it? Who should it help? What should it not be allowed to do?
evidence: Propose at least three rules for a hypothetical AI system they are designing
Explain why AI designers need to think about who might be harmed, not just who benefits
Describe one real example of AI being used responsibly and one where it was not
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was designing an AI assistant for their school, could they think of rules to make sure it was fair and helpful for everyone?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: The Future of AI
topics.description: What AI might do in 10 years; what we want it to do and what we're worried about; children as future designers and decision-makers about AI; hopeful, empowered framing
evidence: Describe at least two ways AI might be used in the future that don't exist yet
Explain one thing they would want AI to do and one thing they would want it not to do
Describe why it matters that young people understand AI — because they will shape how it is used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} have a thoughtful conversation about what they'd want AI to do in the future and what they'd be worried about?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Data and Information for Computers
topics.description: What data is: information that computers use — numbers, words, pictures, sounds; everything a computer knows comes from data that people give it
evidence: Define data as information stored in a computer (numbers, text, images, sounds)
Give at least three examples of data they create every day (photos, messages, search queries)
Explain that a computer only knows what it has been given — it has no knowledge of its own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain what 'data' means and give examples of data they create every time they use a phone or computer?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: All data as numbers
topics.description: Explain how digital systems represent all data — text, images and sound — using numbers: each pixel's colour is stored as numbers, each letter has a number code and sound is stored as a series of number samples
evidence: Colour a pixel grid from a list of numbers (e.g. 0 = white, 1 = black) to reveal a hidden picture
Encode a short word using a number code for letters (e.g. A = 65, B = 66 in ASCII) and decode a partner's word
Explain how a photo, a text message and a song are all stored as numbers in a device
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that a photo on your phone is really stored as numbers — and could they turn a list of numbers into a picture on squared paper?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Binary on and off
topics.description: Explore how digital systems represent data using two states — on and off, written as 1 and 0 — called bits, and use binary numbers to represent whole numbers and letters
evidence: Show every number from 0 to 31 using five binary cards (16, 8, 4, 2, 1) turned face up for 1 and face down for 0
Convert binary numbers such as 1010 and 10011 to ordinary numbers and back
Explain why computers use two states (a switch, light or current is either on or off) and show a letter as a string of bits using a given code
topics.assessmentPrompt: Playing with 'binary cards' or light switches, could {{name}} show how on and off (1 and 0) can make any number — like making 5 with 101?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: How apps meet users' needs
topics.description: Discuss how existing digital systems satisfy the identified needs of known users: what the user needs, which features help and what does not work well for them
evidence: List two needs of a known user (e.g. a younger sibling learning letters needs big buttons and sounds)
Explore an existing app or device and point out the features that meet each need
Say one way the system does not suit the user and suggest a change
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} look at a learning app a younger cousin uses and explain what makes it good for a little kid — like big buttons and sounds — and what could be better?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Problems digital systems solve
topics.description: Investigate simple problems for people they know (classmates, family, the teacher) and suggest how a digital system could help solve them
evidence: Ask a known user (e.g. a classmate, grandparent or teacher) about something they find hard and record it with pictures or words
Suggest a digital system that could help (e.g. a timer app for taking turns, a video call to see a faraway relative, a talking book for a younger sibling)
Explain how the digital system would solve the problem for that person
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} notice a problem someone in the family has — like Grandma missing them — and suggest a device or app that would help, like a video call?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Checking solutions against criteria
topics.description: Discuss how existing digital solutions and their own digital solutions satisfy the design criteria and user stories, using evidence from trying them out
evidence: Try an existing app or game against a checklist of design criteria and user stories and record which are met
Test their own program or digital product with a classmate and record which user stories it satisfies
Discuss one criterion or user story that is not yet met and suggest a change
topics.assessmentPrompt: After making a game or animation, can {{name}} check it against the goals they set — like 'it must have 3 levels' — and say what still needs fixing?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Co-creating user stories
topics.description: Define a problem to be solved with a digital solution using given design criteria, and co-create user stories in the form 'As a ..., I want ..., so that ...' to describe what users need
evidence: Restate a given digital design task (e.g. a quiz game to help Year 1 students learn sight words) as a problem with the given criteria listed
Co-create at least two user stories with a group or a real user (e.g. 'As a Year 1 student, I want to hear each word read aloud, so that I can check I said it correctly')
Check that each user story names the user, what they want and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} was helping design a game for younger kids, could they write a 'user story' like 'As a 6-year-old, I want big buttons so that I can tap them easily'?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Designing a digital solution
topics.description: Generate, communicate and compare designs for a digital solution — sketching or storyboarding the screens, inputs, outputs and steps of a game, app or program — and choose the design that best meets the criteria
evidence: Sketch two different storyboards for a simple game or animation showing each screen, what the user does and what happens
Present a design to a partner, explaining its inputs, outputs and steps
Compare the two designs against the design criteria and user stories and choose one with reasons
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before coding a game, does {{name}} sketch out the screens and what happens when you press each button — and compare a couple of ideas to pick the best?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Designing a user interface
topics.description: Design a user interface for a digital system — the layout of screens, buttons, menus and navigation — applying principles such as consistency, readability and accessibility for the intended users
evidence: Draw wireframes for at least three connected screens of an app or game, showing buttons, menus and how the user moves between screens
Apply interface principles such as consistent button positions, readable text, clear icons and colour contrast, and explain each choice
Test a paper or digital prototype of the interface with a user and note where they got stuck
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} designed the screens for an app, would they think about where the buttons go, how users move between screens and whether it's easy for everyone to use?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Evaluating digital solutions
topics.description: Evaluate existing digital solutions and their own against design criteria and user stories, and consider their broader community impact: who benefits, who might be excluded, and effects on privacy, safety, wellbeing and the environment
evidence: Evaluate their own digital solution against each design criterion and user story using test results and user feedback, rating how well each is met
Evaluate an existing digital solution (e.g. a school app or community website) against criteria they set
Explain the broader community impact of one solution, including who benefits and who could be left out or harmed, and suggest an improvement
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} judge an app — their own or a real one — against the goals it was meant to meet, and think about who in the community it helps or leaves out?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Improving digital designs
topics.description: Generate, modify, communicate and evaluate designs for digital solutions — algorithms, flowcharts, storyboards and wireframes — refining them in response to feedback and testing
evidence: Generate a design for a digital solution using a flowchart for the algorithm and a storyboard or wireframe for the screens
Communicate the design to users or peers in an annotated presentation and collect feedback
Modify the design in response to feedback and evaluate the new version against the design criteria, explaining what improved
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} plans a digital project, do they share their design, take on feedback and improve it — explaining why the new version is better?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: User stories and design criteria
topics.description: Define problems for digital solutions by creating their own user stories for different users and co-developing measurable design criteria from them
evidence: Interview or survey intended users and write user stories for at least two different users of a planned digital solution
Co-develop design criteria from the user stories (e.g. 'A new user can sign up in under one minute') and agree how each will be checked
Write a problem statement that combines the users, their needs and the design criteria
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before making an app or game, could {{name}} talk to the people who'll use it and turn what they need into clear goals the design must meet?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Computers in Everyday Life
topics.description: Identifying computers in everyday life — not just laptops but phones, tablets, smart speakers, traffic lights, washing machines; what makes something a computer
evidence: Point out at least five everyday objects that contain computers
Explain what all computers have in common (they follow instructions and process information)
Sort a set of objects into 'contains a computer' and 'does not contain a computer'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} look around your home and point out at least five things that have a computer inside them, including ones that don't look like traditional computers?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Parts of a computer
topics.description: Identify the components of common digital systems — screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, touchscreen, speakers, microphone and camera — and explore what each is used for, telling parts that put information in (input) from parts that give information out (output)
evidence: Label the screen, keyboard, mouse or trackpad, speaker, microphone and camera on a picture of a laptop or tablet
Use the microphone to record their voice and the speaker to play it back, saying which part takes sound in and which gives it out
Choose the component they would use for a task (e.g. the camera for a photo of a plant, the keyboard to type their name) and explain why
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name the parts of a laptop or tablet — keyboard, screen, camera, microphone, speaker — and say which one they'd use to record a message for Grandma?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Peripherals for different purposes
topics.description: Explore and describe a range of digital systems (computers, tablets, game consoles, smart watches, robots) and the peripherals that connect to them — printers, scanners, headphones, game controllers, external drives, digital microscopes and sensors — and choose peripherals for different purposes
evidence: Connect and use at least two peripherals at school (e.g. headphones and a printer, or a digital microscope) and describe what each adds to the system
Sort peripherals into input, output and storage devices and justify each choice
Recommend a digital system and peripherals for a purpose (e.g. making a class podcast or recording weather data) and explain the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the family wanted to record a podcast or print photos, could {{name}} explain which devices and add-ons you'd need — like a microphone, headphones or a printer — and why?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Sending data between devices
topics.description: Explore how different types of data — text, images, sound and video — are transmitted between digital systems by cable or wirelessly (e.g. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, mobile networks), noticing that larger files such as videos take longer to send
evidence: Send a photo from a tablet to a printer or another device (by cable or wirelessly) and describe the path the data took
Compare sending a text message, a photo and a short video and explain which takes longest and why
Identify whether familiar connections are wired or wireless (e.g. a USB cable, Bluetooth headphones, school Wi-Fi) and give one advantage of each
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sends a photo or video to a relative, can they explain how it gets there — by cable, Bluetooth or Wi-Fi — and why a video takes longer to send than a message?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Computer networks
topics.description: Examine how digital systems connect to form networks — wired and wireless connections, routers and servers in a home or school network — so they can share data and resources such as printers, files and the internet
evidence: Draw a diagram of the school or home network showing devices, the router and wired and wireless links
Explain how a network lets devices share data and resources (e.g. printing from any classroom computer, saving to a shared drive)
Compare a wired and a wireless network connection for speed, reliability and convenience
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain how all the devices at home connect through the Wi-Fi router — and why you can print from any computer in the house?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: How the internet sends data
topics.description: Explain that the internet is a network of networks and that data is broken into small packets, addressed, sent along different routes and reassembled at its destination
evidence: Explain that the internet connects millions of smaller networks around the world
Act out sending a message as packets: split a sentence into numbered cards, pass them by different routes and reassemble them in order
Describe what happens when a packet is lost or arrives late (e.g. a video call freezes) and how numbering helps rebuild the message
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} explain why a video call sometimes freezes — that the internet chops data into little packets that travel separately and are put back together?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Inside a computer
topics.description: Investigate the main internal components of common digital systems — processor (CPU), memory (RAM), storage, circuit board, battery or power supply and wireless adaptor — and explain the function of each
evidence: Identify the processor, memory, storage and battery in a photo or teardown of a computer, tablet or phone
Explain the job of each part using an analogy (e.g. the processor does the work, memory is the desk for things in use, storage is the cupboard for files)
Compare two devices' specifications (e.g. storage size and memory) and explain how they affect what each device can do
topics.assessmentPrompt: Looking at the specs of a new tablet or laptop, could {{name}} explain what the processor, memory and storage each do — and why more storage means more room for photos and games?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Sharing and working together digitally
topics.description: Use the basic features of common digital tools to share content and work together — posting a drawing or recording to a class space, adding to a shared class book or slideshow, giving kind comments — following agreed behaviours with guidance from trusted adults
evidence: Share a photo, drawing or voice recording to a class learning space with teacher guidance
Add their own page or slide to a shared class book without changing anyone else's work
Leave a kind, helpful comment on a classmate's shared work following the class's agreed online behaviours
topics.assessmentPrompt: With a teacher or parent helping, can {{name}} add their page to a shared class book or post a drawing online — and leave a kind comment on someone else's work?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Collaborating in shared documents
topics.description: Use the core features of common digital tools to share content, plan tasks and collaborate — co-editing a shared document or slideshow, using comments and a shared task list — following agreed behaviours with support from trusted adults
evidence: Co-edit a shared document or slideshow with group members, each working on an agreed section
Use comments or suggestions to give feedback instead of deleting a classmate's work
Plan a group task in a shared digital checklist or table showing who does what and by when
topics.assessmentPrompt: Has {{name}} worked on a shared document or slideshow with classmates — each doing their own part and leaving comments rather than deleting others' work?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Saving and organising files
topics.description: Save, name and organise digital files in folders following agreed conventions, so that work can be found, shared and reopened
evidence: Save a piece of work with a meaningful file name following the class convention (e.g. 'Mia_Y4_Frogs_Report')
Create a folder for a topic, move related files into it and find a file again in a later lesson
Follow other agreed conventions for digital work, such as giving image sources, using a consistent heading style and saving a new version instead of overwriting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} save their school work with a sensible file name in the right folder — and find it again the next week?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Choosing the right digital tool
topics.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools effectively to create, locate and communicate content — choosing between word processing, presentation, spreadsheet, graphics, video and search tools for a task, using their digital-specific features and applying common conventions
evidence: Choose the best tool for three tasks (e.g. a budget, a poster, a how-to video) and justify each choice
Use digital-specific features effectively, such as styles and templates, image cropping, spreadsheet formulas or search filters
Apply common conventions such as consistent formatting, file naming, alt text for images and acknowledging sources
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} has a school project, do they pick the right tool — slides for a talk, a spreadsheet for numbers, a video app for a how-to — and use its features well?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Planning digital group projects
topics.description: Select and use appropriate digital tools to share content online, plan tasks and collaborate on projects — task boards, shared calendars, co-edited documents, version history and video calls — demonstrating agreed behaviours
evidence: Choose and justify tools for a group project (e.g. a task board to plan, a shared document to write, a video call to meet)
Plan the project in a digital tool with tasks, owners and deadlines and update progress as work is done
Use version history or comments to track and resolve changes, and share the finished project online safely and respectfully
topics.assessmentPrompt: For a group project, can {{name}} choose sensible online tools — a shared document, a to-do board, a video call — and use them to plan who does what and keep track?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Apps store my data online
topics.description: Discuss that some websites and apps store their personal data online — names, photos, voice recordings, game scores and location — so the information stays there and may be seen by others
evidence: Name personal data a familiar app or game asks for or keeps (e.g. a username, a photo, a score, a location)
Explain that this data is stored on computers far away (online), not just on their own device
Discuss with a trusted adult whether an app really needs the data it asks for before agreeing
topics.assessmentPrompt: When a game or app asks for {{name}}'s name, photo or location, do they understand it gets saved online somewhere — and check with you before typing it in?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Logging in to my account
topics.description: Access their school or learning account using a recorded username and password (e.g. from a login card), log out when finished, and keep the password private except from trusted adults
evidence: Log in to their school account using the username and password on their login card
Log out at the end of a session and explain why (so no-one else can use their account)
Explain that a password is like a key and is only shared with a trusted adult such as a parent or teacher
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} log in to their school learning app using the username and password on their card, and log out when they're finished?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Memorable, hard-to-guess passwords
topics.description: Access their school account using a memorised password and explain why a good password is easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess, avoiding names, birthdays and simple patterns
evidence: Log in to their school account from memory without a login card
Sort example passwords into weak (e.g. 'password', 'ben2015', '1234') and strong (e.g. 'purple-kangaroo-jumps') and explain what makes each easy or hard to guess
Explain why a password must be easy for them to remember but hard for others to guess
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} log in to their school account from memory — and explain why their pet's name or birthday would make a bad password?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: What my accounts store
topics.description: Identify what personal data is stored and shared in their own online accounts (e.g. a school learning account or a game) — profile name, photo, age, location, contacts and work — who can see it, and discuss the associated risks
evidence: Explore the profile and settings of a school or game account with a teacher and list the personal data it stores
Identify who can see each item (only me, my teacher, my class, anyone) and change one privacy setting with adult support
Discuss a risk of sharing data such as a location or full name in a public profile and how to reduce it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Looking at {{name}}'s game or school account together, could they tell you what personal information it stores, who can see it and what the risks might be?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: My digital footprint
topics.description: Explain how their digital footprint is created — posts, photos, comments, searches and data collected by apps — and why it can be permanent, because content can be copied, shared and stored even after it is deleted
evidence: List the parts of their digital footprint from one day (e.g. a search, a game score, a comment, a photo a family member uploaded)
Explain why deleting a post does not guarantee it is gone (others may have copied or shared it, and services keep backups)
Decide whether to post a given photo or comment by thinking about who might see it in five years and justify the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before posting something online, does {{name}} think about the fact that it could be copied and stay around for years — even if they delete it?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Privacy when collecting data
topics.description: Consider privacy when collecting data from users: collect only the data needed, tell people why it is collected, ask permission, avoid identifying details where possible, and store and share results safely
evidence: Review a draft class survey and remove questions that collect unnecessary personal data (e.g. full name, address)
Write a short privacy note for a survey explaining what data is collected, why and who will see it, and ask for permission
Explain how to keep survey results private (e.g. share only totals, store them in a protected folder)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} made an online survey for their class, would they only ask for what they need, explain why, and keep people's answers private?

topics.subject: Computing
topics.name: Unique passphrases
topics.description: Access multiple personal accounts using a unique passphrase for each, and explain the risks of reusing passwords: if one account is breached, every account with the same password is exposed
evidence: Create a passphrase from three or four random words (e.g. 'violin-cactus-ocean-ladder') and explain why its length makes it hard to guess
Log in to at least two different accounts (e.g. a school account and a learning app), each with its own passphrase
Explain what could happen if they used the same password for every account and one website was hacked
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} use a different passphrase for each of their accounts — and can they explain why reusing one password is risky if a website gets hacked?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers up to 10 into pairs
topics.description: Decompose numbers up to 10 into pairs in more than one way (part-part-whole)
evidence: Use objects or drawings to find all pairs that make a given number
Record decompositions as equations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 8 grapes, can they split them into two groups in different ways — like 3 and 5, or 4 and 4 — and explain that both groups together still make 8?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting
topics.description: Add and subtract one-digit and two-digit numbers to 20, including zero
evidence: Calculate 14 + 5 = 19
Calculate 17 – 3 = 14
Add or subtract 0 and explain the result stays the same
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '14 + 5' or '18 − 6' in their head or on paper, and do they know that adding or taking away zero leaves the number unchanged?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Early Word Problems
topics.description: Solve one-step word problems involving addition and subtraction to 20, including missing-number problems
evidence: Solve 'I have 12 sweets and eat 4, how many left?'
Solve missing number: 7 = [ ] – 9
Solve problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'I had some sweets, ate 5, and now have 9 left — how many did I start with?', can {{name}} figure out the missing number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number bonds
topics.description: Recall number bonds (addition and related subtraction facts) within 20
evidence: Quickly recall that 8 + 5 = 13
Given 13 – 5, respond 8 using knowledge of related addition fact
Know all pairs of single-digit numbers that sum to numbers up to 20
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '8 + 7 = 15' and immediately know that '15 − 7 = 8' — without having to work out the subtraction from scratch?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting on screen
topics.description: Partition one-digit numbers and add and subtract within 20 using virtual materials (on-screen ten frames, counters and number lines) as well as physical materials, applying part-part-whole knowledge to 10 and make-ten strategies
evidence: Partition 8 on an on-screen ten frame as 5 and 3 and then as 6 and 2, writing a number sentence for each
Solve 8 + 5 on a virtual double ten frame by moving 2 counters to fill the first frame and adding the remaining 3
Solve 15 - 7 by removing counters on an on-screen twenty frame, then check it with real counters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a maths app with ten frames, can they work out 8 + 5 by filling up the first ten frame — and check it with real counters?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting tens mentally
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 45 + 30 = 75 mentally
Calculate 82 − 40 = 42 mentally
Explain that only the tens digit changes when adding/subtracting tens
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '54 + 30' or '78 − 20' in their head — knowing that only the tens digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Three Small Numbers
topics.description: Add three one-digit numbers using strategies including looking for pairs that make 10
evidence: Calculate 5 + 7 + 3 by first adding 7 + 3 = 10, then 5 + 10 = 15
Add any three single-digit numbers correctly
Identify useful pairs within three addends to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 4 + 6 + 8, can they spot that 4 and 6 make 10 first, then add 8 to get 18 — rather than just adding in order from left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding two two-digit numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mental methods
evidence: Calculate 34 + 27 using base-ten blocks or column addition
Calculate 63 − 28 using a number line or partitioning
Explain a strategy for adding or subtracting two two-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract two two-digit numbers — like '43 + 28' — using counters, a drawing, or working it out in their head?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding within 100
topics.description: Add within 100 using strategies based on place value, including adding a two-digit and one-digit number, and a two-digit and a multiple of 10
evidence: Calculate 46 + 7 using place value (46 + 4 + 3 = 53)
Calculate 38 + 40 = 78 using tens understanding
Relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '47 + 8' or '35 + 50' by thinking about the tens and ones separately rather than counting up one at a time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies
topics.description: Use counting on and counting back as strategies for addition and subtraction
evidence: Add 8 + 3 by starting at 8 and counting on 3 (9, 10, 11)
Subtract 12 − 3 by counting back 3 from 12 (11, 10, 9)
Explain that counting on is a way to add
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 5', can they start from 8 and count up five more — rather than starting from 1 every time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 20
topics.description: Add and subtract within 20 using strategies such as making ten, decomposing a number leading to ten, and using known facts
evidence: Solve 8 + 6 using making ten: 8 + 2 + 4 = 14
Solve 13 − 4 by decomposing: 13 − 3 − 1 = 9
Use a known fact (8 + 4 = 12) to derive 12 − 8 = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '8 + 6', can they split the 6 into 2 + 4, use the 2 to fill up to 10, then add the remaining 4 to get 14?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition in any order
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of addition: addends can be added in any order
evidence: Explain that 3 + 8 gives the same answer as 8 + 3
Use commutativity to choose the larger number to count on from
Demonstrate that subtraction is not commutative (5 − 3 ≠ 3 − 5)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 6 + 4 gives the same answer as 4 + 6, so they can always choose whichever order makes the adding easier?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding a missing number in addition
topics.description: Understand subtraction as finding an unknown addend (e.g. 10 − 8 = ? is the same as 8 + ? = 10)
evidence: Solve 10 − 8 by thinking 'what do I add to 8 to make 10?'
Explain that subtraction can be thought of as a missing-addend problem
Use known addition facts to solve related subtraction problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} see that '10 − 8 = ?' is the same as asking 'what do I add to 8 to reach 10?' — so they can use their adding knowledge to help with subtraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 10
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 10
evidence: Answer any addition fact within 10 quickly from memory
Answer any subtraction fact within 10 quickly from memory
Complete a timed set of within-10 facts with high accuracy
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer sums like '7 + 3' or '9 − 4' almost instantly — without stopping to count on their fingers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction
topics.description: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100
evidence: Rapidly recall 7 + 8 = 15 and 15 − 8 = 7
Use 6 + 4 = 10 to derive 60 + 40 = 100
Derive 35 + 5 = 40 from knowledge that 5 + 5 = 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts like '9 + 7 = 16' and '16 − 7 = 9', and use those to help work out bigger sums like '90 + 70'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Grouping numbers to add
topics.description: Understand and apply the associative property of addition: when adding three numbers, any two can be added first
evidence: Solve 2 + 6 + 4 by first adding 6 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 10 = 12
Explain that grouping addends differently gives the same total
Choose which two numbers to add first to make the calculation easier
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 3 + 7 + 6, can they spot that adding 3 and 7 first (to make 10) is easier — rather than always working left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Inverse: addition undoes subtraction
topics.description: Recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations and solve missing-number problems
evidence: Check 15 + 7 = 22 by calculating 22 − 7 = 15
Use the inverse to solve: □ + 9 = 14, so □ = 14 − 9 = 5
Explain that addition and subtraction 'undo' each other
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out 13 + 5 = 18, can they immediately use that to say '18 − 5 = 13' — without having to work the subtraction out all over again?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 6+)
topics.description: Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones mentally and using concrete/pictorial representations
evidence: Calculate 36 + 7 = 43 using objects or mentally
Calculate 52 − 4 = 48 using a number line or mentally
Explain bridging through 10 when adding ones to a two-digit number
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '36 + 7' or '42 − 5' in their head — keeping the tens in place and only adjusting the ones?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental and written addition and subtraction
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems using mental and written methods, including problems involving numbers, quantities, and measures
evidence: Solve a two-step problem: 'I had 35p, spent 12p, then found 5p. How much now?'
Choose an appropriate method (mental or written) for a given problem
Solve problems involving measures, e.g. 'a ribbon is 45cm, I cut off 18cm'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a problem involving lengths, weights, or prices, can they decide whether to add or subtract and carry out the calculation correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Subtracting multiples of 10
topics.description: Subtract multiples of 10 (10–90) from multiples of 10 using place value strategies
evidence: Calculate 70 − 30 = 40
Use base-ten blocks to show 80 − 50 = 30
Explain that subtracting tens is like subtracting the tens digits
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '80 − 50' or '70 − 40' in their head by thinking about how many tens are left?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Three-number word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems that call for adding three whole numbers with a total of 20 or less, representing the problem with objects, a drawing or a three-part bar model and with an equation that uses a symbol for the unknown total (e.g. 4 + 7 + 6 = ☐); choose a convenient order or grouping to add (such as making 10 first) and give the answer in the context of the problem
evidence: Solve 'Sam has 4 red, 7 blue and 6 green pencils. How many pencils does he have?' with counters or a drawing, writing 4 + 7 + 6 = ☐ and answering 'Sam has 17 pencils'
Write the equation 3 + 9 + 7 = ☐ for a story about apples picked on three days, and add 3 + 7 first to make 10 (19 apples)
Draw a three-part bar model for a story about 5 cars, 8 bikes and 2 buses and explain how each part matches a number in the equation 5 + 8 + 2 = ☐
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} picks 4 apples, then 7, then 6, could they show the problem with objects or a drawing, write it as 4 + 7 + 6 = ?, and work out how many apples they have altogether?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unknown in Addition & Subtraction
topics.description: Determine the unknown whole number in an addition or subtraction equation relating three whole numbers
evidence: Solve 8 + ? = 11 and write 3
Solve 5 = □ − 3 and write 8
Solve 6 + 6 = □ and write 12
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '? + 6 = 14' or '9 − ? = 4' written on paper, can they figure out what number goes in the gap?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What the equals sign means
topics.description: Understand the meaning of the equal sign as 'is the same as' and determine if equations are true or false
evidence: Explain that 6 = 6 is true because both sides are the same
Determine that 4 + 1 = 5 + 2 is false
Understand that = does not mean 'the answer comes next' — it means balance
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} understand that '=' means 'the same as', so they can tell you whether '4 + 3 = 8 − 1' is true or false?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 7+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers with up to three digits using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction
evidence: Set out a columnar addition correctly with digits aligned by place value
Carry out columnar subtraction with exchange (borrowing) when needed
Check the answer using the inverse operation or estimation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} set out a sum like '347 + 265' or '512 − 278' in columns and work through it step by step, carrying or borrowing where needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding numbers
topics.description: Add up to four two-digit numbers using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
evidence: Add three or four two-digit numbers by grouping tens and ones
Look for pairs that make multiples of 10 to simplify addition
Explain the strategy used to combine multiple addends
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add up four two-digit numbers — like '14 + 23 + 32 + 19' — by grouping them cleverly, rather than just plodding through from left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies (age 7+)
topics.description: Explain why addition and subtraction strategies work, using place value and the properties of operations
evidence: Explain why adding tens and ones separately gives the correct total
Describe why a compensation strategy works (e.g. 'I added 1 too many, so I subtract 1')
Use place-value language to justify a written method step by step
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out '67 + 24' by splitting it into '60 + 20' and '7 + 4', can they explain to you in words *why* that approach gives the right answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction within 1000
topics.description: Add and subtract within 1000 using concrete models, drawings, and strategies based on place value; understand composing and decomposing tens and hundreds
evidence: Add two three-digit numbers using base-ten blocks or drawings, composing a ten or hundred when necessary
Subtract three-digit numbers, decomposing a ten or hundred when necessary
Relate the concrete/drawn strategy to a written method and explain why it works
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract numbers in the hundreds — like '347 + 256' — by thinking about hundreds, tens, and ones separately, or drawing a diagram to help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating by rounding
topics.description: Estimate the answer to a calculation and use inverse operations to check answers; apply to increasingly large numbers using rounding and inverse reasoning
evidence: Round numbers to the nearest 10 or 100 to estimate a sum or difference before calculating
Use addition to check a subtraction answer, or vice versa
Identify when a calculated answer is unreasonable based on the estimate
Round numbers to estimate a sum or difference before calculating
Use addition to check a subtraction answer and vice versa
Identify an unreasonable answer by comparing to the estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} works out a calculation, can they make a sensible rough guess — and then check their answer using the opposite operation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 100
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 100 using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction
evidence: Add two-digit numbers within 100 efficiently (e.g. 46 + 37 using place-value partitioning)
Subtract two-digit numbers within 100 fluently (e.g. 83 − 25)
Choose between strategies (decomposing, compensating, using known facts) based on the numbers involved
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} reliably add or subtract two-digit numbers like '68 + 27' or '91 − 45', choosing the best strategy for each problem?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 20
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 20 using mental strategies; know from memory all sums of two one-digit numbers
evidence: Answer any single-digit addition fact within 3 seconds
Recall subtraction facts within 20 from memory (e.g. 15 − 8 = 7)
Use known addition facts to derive related subtraction facts rapidly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} instantly recall all the single-digit addition facts — like '7 + 8 = 15' — without needing to count or think for more than a second?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 7+)
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and ones
evidence: Calculate 345 + 7 mentally
Calculate 462 − 5 mentally
Explain that only the ones digit changes (unless bridging through a ten)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '436 + 7' or '521 − 8' in their head — keeping the hundreds and tens unchanged while adjusting just the ones?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mentally adding hundreds to 3-digit numbers
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and hundreds
evidence: Calculate 345 + 200 mentally
Calculate 762 − 400 mentally
Explain that only the hundreds digit changes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '342 + 200' or '756 − 300' in their head — knowing that only the hundreds digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mentally adding tens to 3-digit numbers
topics.description: Mentally add and subtract a three-digit number and tens
evidence: Calculate 345 + 40 mentally
Calculate 462 − 30 mentally
Explain that only the tens digit changes (unless bridging through a hundred)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '354 + 40' or '628 − 30' in their head — knowing that only the tens digit changes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Missing number problems (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction problems including missing-number problems, using number facts, place value, and more complex methods
evidence: Solve a missing-number problem such as 245 + ? = 380
Choose an appropriate method (mental, written, or combination) based on the numbers
Solve multi-step problems combining addition and subtraction of three-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums with a hidden number — like '? − 38 = 24' or '53 + ? = 91' — by thinking carefully about what the equation is asking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Represent whole numbers as lengths on a number line and represent sums and differences within 100 on a number line diagram
evidence: Place whole numbers on a number line with equally spaced points
Show an addition as a jump forward on the number line (e.g. 38 + 27 shown as jumps)
Show a subtraction as a jump backward on the number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} mark numbers on a number line and show what happens when they add or subtract — for example, jumping forward 35 places from 48?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-Step Word Problems
topics.description: Solve one- and two-step word problems within 100 using addition and subtraction, with unknowns in all positions
evidence: Solve a two-step word problem involving adding to and taking from
Represent a word problem with an equation using a symbol for the unknown
Solve comparison problems (how many more/fewer) within 100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a word problem says 'Sam had 78 stickers, gave some away, and now has 45 — how many did he give away?', can {{name}} work out which operation to use and find the answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 8+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers with up to four digits using formal written methods of columnar addition and subtraction
evidence: Set out and solve a columnar addition with up to four-digit numbers
Set out and solve a columnar subtraction with exchange across multiple columns
Check the answer using estimation or inverse operations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} line up a sum like '3,842 + 1,765' or '4,301 − 2,658' in columns and work through it correctly — carrying and borrowing across multiple columns?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent adding and subtracting within 1000
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract within 1000 using strategies and algorithms based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction
evidence: Add two three-digit numbers fluently using an efficient method
Subtract three-digit numbers fluently, including with regrouping
Choose the most efficient strategy based on the numbers involved
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract three-digit numbers like '672 − 348' reliably, choosing whichever method works best for them?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-step addition and subtraction problems
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction two-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why
evidence: Identify the two steps needed to solve a contextual problem
Choose between mental and written methods for each step based on the numbers
Explain why the chosen operations and methods are appropriate
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads a word problem with two steps — like working out change from a shopping trip with two items — can they plan which calculations to do and in what order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Two-Step Equations
topics.description: Solve two-step word problems using the four operations; represent problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity
evidence: Solve a two-step problem that combines addition/subtraction with multiplication/division
Write an equation using a letter for the unknown (e.g. 3 × n + 5 = 26)
Assess the reasonableness of the answer using estimation and mental computation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} write an equation like 'n + 25 = 60' to represent a word problem, and then solve it to find what n equals?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why
evidence: A school collects 12,450 bottles in Week 1 and 8,372 in Week 2; their target is 25,000 — how many more do they need?
Choose between mental and written methods for each step and explain why
Solve a three-step problem involving addition and subtraction of five-digit numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem — like planning a budget where money is added and spent in several steps — can they decide which operations to use at each stage and explain their thinking?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Checking Answers by Rounding
topics.description: Use rounding to check answers to calculations and determine appropriate levels of accuracy in context
evidence: Check 47,832 + 23,156 ≈ 48,000 + 23,000 = 71,000 to verify the exact answer 70,988
Decide whether to round to the nearest 100 or 1,000 for a given estimation context
Identify that a calculated answer of 3,421 cannot be correct because the estimate gives approximately 50,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} gets an answer of 4,213 for an addition, can they round the numbers to double-check — like '4,000 + 1,000 ≈ 5,000' — and spot if the answer seems way off?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent addition and subtraction (age 9+)
topics.description: Fluently add and subtract whole numbers with more than four digits using the standard columnar algorithm
evidence: Calculate 34,567 + 28,945 using columnar addition
Calculate 500,000 − 234,178 using columnar subtraction with multiple exchanges
Add three five-digit numbers in a single column layout
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} accurately add or subtract large numbers — like '23,846 + 14,579' — using the column method, carrying and borrowing correctly however many columns it takes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental addition and subtraction (age 9+)
topics.description: Add and subtract numbers mentally with increasingly large numbers, using place-value knowledge and derived facts
evidence: Mentally calculate 45,000 + 8,000
Mentally subtract 3,200 from 10,000 by counting up
Use near-doubles: 2,500 + 2,600 = 5,100
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out something like '4,700 − 1,300' in their head using what they know about place value — without needing to write it all out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting (age 10+)
topics.description: Solve addition and subtraction multi-step problems in contexts, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, with numbers up to 10,000,000 and decimals
evidence: Solve a two-step word problem involving addition and subtraction of numbers beyond 1,000,000
Choose between mental, written, and calculator methods for a multi-step problem and justify the choice
Interpret a real-life context to identify which addition/subtraction operations are needed across multiple steps
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a complicated word problem involving large numbers or decimals — like calculating the total cost of several items — can they plan and carry out all the steps correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction strategies (age 10+)
topics.description: Add and subtract decimals to hundredths using strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate strategies to written methods and explain reasoning
evidence: Correctly compute 3.45 + 2.78 and explain regrouping across decimal places
Use a number line or base-ten blocks to model 5.03 − 2.67
Explain why the standard algorithm works for decimal addition by connecting to place-value understanding
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} add or subtract decimal amounts like '4.73 + 2.68' or '10.00 − 3.47', lining up the decimal points and working through the columns correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Positive and Negative Numbers
topics.description: Understand positive and negative numbers as describing quantities with opposite directions or values; use them in context such as temperature, floors in a building, and bank balances
evidence: Represent positive and negative numbers on a number line and explain what zero means in context
Add a positive or negative number to any integer using number line reasoning
Subtract a positive or negative number from any integer, understanding that subtracting a negative is equivalent to adding
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees temperatures like −3°C and +5°C on a weather forecast, can they figure out how much warmer one day is than the other — even when the answer crosses zero?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding the repeating unit
topics.description: Identify and describe the repeating unit (core) of a repeating pattern made with numbers, symbols, shapes or objects, and use it to continue, create and compare patterns
evidence: Circle the part that repeats in red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue and describe it as an ABB pattern
Build a new pattern with the unit 1, 2, 2, 3 and repeat it three times
Say whether clap, stamp, stamp, clap, stamp, stamp and circle, square, square have the same repeating unit
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees beads threaded red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue, can they point out the part that keeps repeating and use it to make their own pattern?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Describing growing number patterns
topics.description: Recognise, describe and create additive patterns that increase or decrease by a constant amount using numbers, shapes and objects, state the rule, and find missing elements
evidence: Describe 5, 8, 11, 14 as 'start at 5 and add 3 each time'
Find the missing numbers in 40, 35, __, 25, __, 15
Build a tower pattern that grows by 2 blocks each step and predict the 6th tower
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the house numbers 5, 8, 11, 14 along a street, can they say the numbers go up by 3 each time and work out what comes next?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Following number algorithms
topics.description: Follow and create algorithms (flowcharts or written step lists) with a sequence of steps, decisions using comparisons (e.g. 'Is the number greater than 20?', 'Is it even?') and repetition until a stop condition, to investigate numbers and describe the patterns that emerge
evidence: Follow a flowchart: start at 7; if the number is even halve it, otherwise add 1; repeat until you reach 1, and record each number
Describe what a flowchart with the decision 'Is the number greater than 50?' does to the numbers 34, 51 and 80
Write a step-by-step algorithm with one decision that sorts a list of numbers into 'less than 10' and '10 or more'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a set of instructions like 'if the number is even, halve it; if it's odd, add 1; keep going until you reach 1', can they follow it step by step and notice any pattern?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Algorithms that generate number sets
topics.description: Follow and create algorithms with steps and decisions that use addition or multiplication to generate sets of numbers (e.g. repeated doubling or adding a constant until a limit), and identify and describe the patterns produced
evidence: Follow 'start at 3, double the number, stop when it is greater than 100' and list the numbers made
Create an algorithm that adds 7 repeatedly from 0 and stops before 80, then describe the pattern in the ones digits
Explain why an algorithm that multiplies by 5 always produces numbers ending in 0 or 5
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} follows the rule 'start at 3 and keep doubling until you go past 100', can they list the numbers and spot a pattern in them?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Designing number algorithms
topics.description: Design and use algorithms with a sequence of steps, decisions with several alternatives (if / else-if / else) and repetition that apply rules to generate sets of numbers, implementing them in a flowchart, spreadsheet or visual program, and explain the patterns produced
evidence: Design a flowchart that classifies each number from 1 to 30 as 'multiple of 3', 'multiple of 5', 'both' or 'neither' and repeats for every number
Implement 'start at 1; repeat 10 times: multiply by 2 and add 1' in a spreadsheet or block program and list the numbers made
Explain why every number generated by the 'multiply by 2 and add 1' algorithm is odd
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} design a set of instructions — like a flowchart or a simple spreadsheet — that sorts every number from 1 to 30 into groups such as 'multiple of 3', 'multiple of 5' or 'both', and explain the pattern?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equations with Two Unknowns
topics.description: Find pairs of numbers that satisfy an equation with two unknowns (e.g. find pairs (a, b) where a + b = 10 or 2a + b = 15)
evidence: List all whole-number pairs (a, b) where a + b = 12 with a, b > 0
Find three pairs that satisfy 2x + y = 20
Explain systematically how to generate all integer solutions to a two-variable equation within a given range
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find different pairs of numbers that both satisfy a rule — for example, all the pairs of whole numbers that add up to 10?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Linear number sequences
topics.description: Generate and describe linear number sequences, including those with negative and decimal steps; identify the term-to-term rule
evidence: Continue the sequence 2.5, 4.0, 5.5, ... and state the rule as 'add 1.5'
Generate terms of a sequence that crosses zero (e.g. 3, 1, −1, −3, ...)
Describe the term-to-term rule for a given linear sequence and predict the 10th term
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a number sequence like 3, 7, 11, 15… can they describe the rule, continue it, and predict what the 10th number will be?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Number Pattern Relationships
topics.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules; identify relationships between corresponding terms; form ordered pairs and graph them on a coordinate plane
evidence: Generate sequences starting at 0 with rules 'add 3' and 'add 6'; observe terms in one are twice the other
Form ordered pairs from corresponding terms and plot them on a coordinate grid
Explain informally why the relationship between the two sequences holds
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} follow two number patterns at once — for example, "add 2" and "add 4" — pair up the matching terms, and plot those pairs as points on a graph?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Systematic Listing
topics.description: Enumerate possibilities of combinations of two variables systematically (e.g. all ways to choose from a set of options)
evidence: List all possible meal combinations from 3 starters and 4 mains
Organise combinations into a systematic table to ensure none are missed
Explain why the total number of combinations equals the product of the options in each category
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} can choose any combination of 3 T-shirt colours and 2 trouser colours, can they list every possible outfit without missing any or repeating?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using Simple Formulae
topics.description: Use simple formulae expressed in words or symbols to calculate values (e.g. perimeter = 2 × (length + width))
evidence: Substitute values into P = 2(l + w) to find the perimeter of a rectangle
Use the formula for area of a triangle (A = 1/2 × b × h) given base and height values
Interpret a formula expressed in words and use it to compute an output
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told that the perimeter of a rectangle uses the formula perimeter = 2 × (length + width), can they plug in the measurements and work out the answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing Algebraic Equations
topics.description: Express missing number problems algebraically using letters for unknowns; translate word problems into equations
evidence: Write 'I think of a number, double it, and add 5 to get 17' as 2n + 5 = 17
Solve a one-step equation such as 3x = 24 and explain the reasoning
Express a word problem as an algebraic equation and find the unknown value
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads "I think of a number, double it, and add 5 to get 17," can they write that as an equation using a letter for the unknown and solve it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Algebraic Notation
topics.description: Use and interpret algebraic notation including: ab for a × b, 3y for y + y + y, a² for a × a, a/b for a ÷ b, coefficients as fractions, and brackets for grouping; read and write algebraic expressions fluently
evidence: Read and interpret expressions using standard algebraic conventions for multiplication, division, and powers
Write algebraic expressions from word descriptions using correct notation
Understand that juxtaposition means multiplication and that a/b means a divided by b
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} sees something written as "3y" or "a²" in a maths problem, do they know what those shorthand notations mean and can they work with them?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Algebraic Transformations
topics.description: Model situations or procedures by translating them into algebraic expressions or formulae and by using graphs; move between word problems, algebraic representations, tables, and graphical representations
evidence: Translate a word problem or real-world situation into an algebraic expression or formula
