Construct a table of values from an algebraic rule
Plot the corresponding graph and interpret it in the context of the problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} take a real-world situation — like a taxi that charges £2 plus £1.50 per mile — and write an algebraic formula for the total cost, then sketch what the graph looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Collecting Like Terms
topics.description: Simplify algebraic expressions by collecting like terms — combine terms with the same variable and power (e.g., 3a + 2b + 5a = 8a + 2b) while maintaining equivalence
evidence: Identify like terms in an algebraic expression
Combine like terms involving positive and negative coefficients
Simplify expressions involving multiple variables and constant terms
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an expression like "5a + 3b + 2a," can they simplify it by collecting the like terms to get "7a + 3b"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Coordinates (age 11+)
topics.description: Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane, using positive and negative x- and y-values to describe positions precisely
evidence: Plot points with negative coordinates accurately in all four quadrants
Identify the quadrant a point belongs to from its coordinate signs
Read coordinates from a graph including fractional and negative values
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} plot a point like (−3, 4) correctly on a coordinate grid and read the coordinates of points in all four quadrants, including negative numbers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expanding Single Brackets
topics.description: Expand (multiply out) a single term over a bracket using the distributive property, e.g., 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15; expand expressions involving negative multipliers
evidence: Multiply a single positive term over a bracket to expand the expression
Multiply a negative term over a bracket, correctly handling signs
Combine expanding brackets with collecting like terms to simplify fully
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} expand a bracket like 3(2x + 5) by multiplying everything inside, to get 6x + 15?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Expressions & Equations Vocabulary
topics.description: Understand and use the concepts and vocabulary of expressions, equations, inequalities, terms, and factors; distinguish between an expression (no equals sign), an equation (equals sign), and an inequality (inequality sign)
evidence: Define and distinguish between expression, equation, and inequality
Identify terms, coefficients, and factors in algebraic expressions
Use the vocabulary of algebra precisely in mathematical discussions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain the difference between an expression like "3x + 2," an equation like "3x + 2 = 11," and an inequality like "3x + 2 > 11"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Generating Sequences
topics.description: Generate terms of a sequence from a term-to-term rule (e.g., 'add 3 each time') or a position-to-term rule (e.g., '2n + 1'), and identify whether a sequence is arithmetic, geometric, or neither
evidence: Continue a sequence given a term-to-term rule involving addition, subtraction, or multiplication
Generate the first five terms from a position-to-term formula such as 3n − 2
Classify sequences as arithmetic (constant difference), geometric (constant ratio), or other
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out the next few terms of a sequence like 5, 8, 11, 14… and explain whether the rule is "add a fixed number each time" or something else?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Numbers on a number line
topics.description: Understand inequalities as statements comparing expressions, represent solutions on a number line, and solve simple linear inequalities using the same inverse-operation methods as equations
evidence: Write an inequality from a worded constraint (e.g., 'must be at least 12' → x ≥ 12)
Represent the solution set of an inequality on a number line with open or closed circles
Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} solve an inequality like 2x + 1 < 9, show the answer on a number line, and explain what all the solutions have in common?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Solving Linear Equations
topics.description: Use algebraic methods to solve linear equations in one variable, including equations that require rearrangement, expanding brackets, and collecting terms on both sides; solve equations with rational number coefficients
evidence: Solve one-step and two-step linear equations in one variable
Solve equations requiring expansion of brackets and collection of like terms
Solve equations with the unknown on both sides and with fractional or negative coefficients
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an equation like 3x + 7 = 22, can they work through the steps to find the value of x?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Substituting into Formulae
topics.description: Substitute numerical values into formulae and expressions including scientific formulae; evaluate expressions by replacing variables with given values and computing the result using correct order of operations
evidence: Substitute positive and negative values into algebraic expressions and evaluate
Substitute values into formulae involving multiple operations and powers
Use correct order of operations when evaluating expressions after substitution
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a formula says that the area of a triangle is ½ × base × height, can {{name}} substitute in the measurements and calculate the answer correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factorising Expressions
topics.description: Factorise algebraic expressions by taking out common factors — identify the highest common factor of all terms and write the expression as a product, e.g., 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
evidence: Identify the highest common factor of all terms in an expression
Write the factorised form as a product of the HCF and a bracket
Check factorisation by expanding the brackets back out
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at an expression like "6x + 9" and rewrite it with the common factor taken out — as "3(2x + 3)"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Linear Function Graphs
topics.description: Recognise that a linear function produces a straight-line graph, understand the relationship between an equation of the form y = mx + c and its graphical representation, and interpret gradient and y-intercept in context
evidence: Explain that changing m in y = mx + c alters the steepness and direction of the line
Identify the y-intercept of a line from its equation and from its graph
Determine whether a given equation will produce a straight line or a curve
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the equation y = 2x + 3, can they explain what the graph will look like — including how steep it is and where it crosses the y-axis?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Nth-Term Rules
topics.description: Find the nth-term expression for an arithmetic sequence by identifying the common difference and the zero-term, and use it to determine any term in the sequence or test whether a given number belongs to the sequence
evidence: Derive the nth-term rule for an arithmetic sequence such as 3, 7, 11, 15, … as 4n − 1
Use an nth-term formula to find the 50th or 100th term without listing all preceding terms
Determine whether a given number (e.g., 99) is a term in a specified arithmetic sequence
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given the sequence 4, 7, 10, 13…, can they find a formula for the nth term — and use it to check whether, say, 100 is in the sequence?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Plotting Linear Graphs
topics.description: Plot linear graphs by generating a table of values, reduce a two-variable linear equation to the form y = mx + c, and calculate gradients from two points on a line
evidence: Generate a table of (x, y) values for a linear equation and plot the points accurately
Rearrange an equation such as 2x + 3y = 12 into the form y = mx + c
Calculate the gradient between two coordinate points using rise over run
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw the graph of a straight line by making a table of values and plotting the points — and work out the gradient from two points on the line?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple formulae
topics.description: Understand and use standard mathematical formulae; rearrange formulae to change the subject, performing inverse operations to isolate a different variable
evidence: Identify the subject of a given formula
Use inverse operations to rearrange a formula to make a different variable the subject
Rearrange formulae involving multiple steps including fractions and powers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a formula gives speed as distance ÷ time, can {{name}} rearrange it to find distance or time when they're the unknowns instead?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 2s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 2, 5, and 10 (skip counting)
evidence: Count 2, 4, 6, 8 … up to at least 20
Count 5, 10, 15, 20 … up to at least 50
Count 10, 20, 30 … up to 100
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is counting socks being paired up, can they skip-count in twos — 2, 4, 6, 8 — all the way to 20? Can they also count up in fives when counting coins, or in tens on a number line?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting big collections in groups
topics.description: Quantify collections of up to 120 objects by partitioning them into equal groups (twos, fives or tens) and skip counting, explaining why grouping makes counting faster and more reliable
evidence: Count 85 pegs by sorting them into groups of ten and counting on 10, 20, ... 80, 85
Count 46 shoes by pairing them and skip counting by twos
Explain why counting 120 straws in bundles of ten is easier than counting one by one
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to know how many pasta shells are in a big jar, can they put them into groups of ten and count the groups to find the total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in steps of 3 from 0
evidence: Count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 … up to at least 30
Count backwards in 3s from 30
Identify the next number in a sequence of multiples of 3
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in threes — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — far enough to reach 30 without losing track or needing to start over?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting forwards and backwards (age 6+)
topics.description: Count forwards and backwards in tens from any number (not just multiples of 10)
evidence: Count 7, 17, 27, 37 … from a non-multiple starting point
Count backwards in tens from 83
Explain the pattern of adding/subtracting 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts at 37 and you ask them to count up in tens, can they say 37, 47, 57, 67 — crossing over into the next hundred without getting stuck?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Within 1,000
topics.description: Count within 1000, including skip-counting by 5s, 10s, and 100s
evidence: Count forwards and backwards within 1000 from any starting number
Skip-count by 5s from any multiple of 5 to 1000
Skip-count by 100s from any number (e.g. 150, 250, 350 …)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count confidently up to 1000 — and if you ask them to count by hundreds from 200, or by tens from 650, can they do it without losing their place?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Skip Counting (4s, 8s, 50s, 100s)
topics.description: Count from 0 in multiples of 4, 8, 50, and 100
evidence: Recite the multiples of 4 from 0 to at least 48
Recite the multiples of 8 from 0 to at least 96
Count in steps of 50 and 100 from 0 to 1000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in fours all the way to 48, count in eights, or count up in hundreds from any starting point — for example 350, 450, 550?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting in 6s
topics.description: Count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25, and 1000
evidence: Recite the multiples of 6 from 0 to at least 72
Recite the multiples of 7 from 0 to at least 84
Count in steps of 25 from 0 to 1000 and in steps of 1000 up to 10,000
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} count in sevens — 7, 14, 21, 28 — or in nines, or in 25s when thinking about coins, or in 1000s when talking about distances like kilometres?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts
topics.description: Interpret and construct simple pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, and simple tables
evidence: Read a pictogram where each symbol represents one item
Construct a tally chart from collected data
Draw a block diagram to represent data from a survey
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a simple chart or pictogram — like one showing how many children chose each favourite fruit — and answer questions like "which was most popular"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Data with digital tools
topics.description: Use simple digital tools (graphing apps, tablet tally counters) to acquire and record categorical data from surveys, observations and simple experiments, display it as a list, table, picture or bar graph, and compare category frequencies
evidence: Enter class votes for favourite fruit into a graphing app to make a picture graph and say which fruit has the most and the fewest votes
Record a tally of birds seen using a tablet counting tool
Drop a paper cup 10 times, record whether it lands upright, upside down or on its side in a tablet tally app, and list the results in a table
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} uses a tablet app at school to record a class vote, can they turn the results into a simple graph and say which choice was most popular?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 6+)
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of data collection and display — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart — and apply these terms when collecting, organising, and presenting data
evidence: Correctly label the axes of a bar chart including a title, axis labels, and scale
Distinguish between discrete data (counted) and continuous data (measured) with an example of each
Use 'tally', 'frequency', and 'pictogram' correctly when describing how to record and display data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wanted to show you how many books different children in their class read last month, could they draw a bar chart, label the axes, and explain what each bar represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Picture & Bar Graphs
topics.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories; solve put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph
evidence: Draw a picture graph with a symbol representing one unit for each data point
Draw a bar graph with labelled axes and a single-unit scale
Use a bar graph to answer comparison questions (e.g. 'How many more votes did cats get than dogs?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw a simple bar chart or picture graph to show information — like how many of each colour of sweet are in a bag — and answer questions from it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting Data into Categories
topics.description: Organise and represent data with up to three categories by counting objects in each category and sorting categories by quantity
evidence: Sort a set of objects into 2-3 given categories and count each group
Create a simple table or list showing category names and counts
Order categories from most to fewest or fewest to most
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at a collection of objects — like different coloured counters — sort them into up to three groups, count each group, and organise the results into a simple chart?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sorting into categories (age 6+)
topics.description: Interpret categorical data by asking and answering questions about totals, how many in each category, and how many more or less one category has than another
evidence: Answer 'how many?' for each category in a data set
Calculate the total number of data points across all categories
Compare two categories using 'how many more/fewer' language
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a chart showing how many children chose each flavour of ice cream, can they answer questions like "how many chose chocolate?" and "how many more chose vanilla than strawberry?"

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing two data displays
topics.description: Compare different graphical representations of the same data (tally chart, picture graph, bar graph, list) and identify and describe the features each shows in response to questions
evidence: Show the same pet survey as a tally chart and as a picture graph and say what is the same in both
Explain which display makes it quicker to see the most popular pet
Answer the same question ('How many chose dogs?') from two different displays of the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a class pet survey shown as both a tally chart and a picture graph, can they explain what both show and which one makes the favourite easier to spot?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Bar graphs
topics.description: Interpret and present discrete and continuous data using appropriate graphical methods, including bar charts and time graphs
evidence: Read a time graph showing temperature changes over a day
Present data about plant growth over weeks as a time graph
Explain the difference between a bar chart (discrete) and a time graph (continuous)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} choose the right type of chart for some data — for example, a bar chart for favourite colours or a line graph for temperature over a week — and draw it correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Choosing displays for a purpose
topics.description: Create and compare different representations of the same data set (table, scaled pictograph, bar graph), including with software, interpret the data in context, and choose the representation that best suits a purpose
evidence: Show the same sport survey as a table and as a bar graph made in software and describe what each makes easy to see
Choose a table to read an exact count and a bar graph to compare categories at a glance, explaining both choices
Interpret the bar graph by saying which sport is most popular and by how much
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has survey results, can they explain when a table is better (finding exact numbers) and when a bar graph is better (comparing at a glance)?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Collecting data for a question
topics.description: Acquire categorical and discrete numerical data to address a question of interest by observing, collecting or accessing a data set, and record it using appropriate methods including frequency tables and spreadsheets
evidence: Collect data on how students travel to school to answer 'What is the most common way to get to school?'
Record the number of siblings each classmate has in a frequency table with tallies and totals
Enter the same data into a spreadsheet with one column for the category and one for the count
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to find out the most popular way kids get to school, can they plan what to ask, collect the answers, and record them neatly in a table?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Guided statistical investigation
topics.description: Carry out a guided statistical investigation for a question of interest: collect categorical or discrete numerical data, represent it in a suitable display and interpret the results in terms of the question
evidence: With guidance, investigate 'Which playground equipment is used most at lunch?' by tallying observations over three days
Represent the results in a bar graph with a title and labelled axes
Write two sentences answering the investigation question using the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class asks 'Which fruit do we eat most at recess?', can they help collect the data, make a graph, and say what the results show?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Scaled picture and bar graphs
topics.description: Draw a scaled picture graph and a scaled bar graph to represent a data set; solve one- and two-step comparison, sum, and difference problems using bar charts, pictograms, and tables
evidence: Draw a bar graph where each square represents 5 pets
From a scaled pictogram, answer: how many more children chose football than tennis?
Solve a two-step problem: how many votes in total for the top two choices?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a bar chart showing how many books different children read last month, could they work out the total, find the difference between the most and least, and draw their own chart with a scale like "each square = 2 books"?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Collecting data with digital tools
topics.description: Use digital tools (online survey forms, spreadsheets, data-logging apps) to acquire categorical and discrete numerical data that address a question of interest, and display it as a column graph or other visualisation
evidence: Create an online survey question to find classmates' favourite sport and collect the responses
Enter survey results in a spreadsheet and make a column graph from them
Interpret the digital graph by describing the most and least popular choices
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to survey their class, can they use a simple online form or spreadsheet to collect the answers and turn them into a graph?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing displays and distributions
topics.description: Analyse how effectively different displays or visualisations show and compare data distributions, and describe the shape of a distribution and the variation in the data
evidence: Compare a column graph and a pictograph of the same data and explain which shows the differences between categories more clearly
Describe a dot plot of hand spans as 'most values cluster around 16 cm with a few much larger'
Explain which display best compares the heights of two classes and why
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees the same results shown in two different graphs, can they explain which graph shows the pattern more clearly and describe where most of the results sit?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Conducting a statistical investigation
topics.description: Conduct a statistical investigation by collecting data through survey responses and other methods, recording and displaying the data with digital tools, and interpreting and communicating the results
evidence: Design a 3-question survey about screen time and collect responses from at least 15 people
Record the responses in a spreadsheet and create a suitable graph
Present two findings to the class, using the graph as evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} run their own survey — like asking friends about screen time — put the answers into a spreadsheet graph, and explain what they found?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graph problems
topics.description: Solve comparison, sum, and difference problems using information presented in a line graph
evidence: Read a line graph of temperature over a week and identify the warmest day
Find the difference in rainfall between two months from a line graph
Explain what a rising/falling line means on a time-series graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a line graph showing how a plant's height changed over several weeks, can they read off values, spot when it grew fastest, and find the difference between two points?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading tables
topics.description: Complete, read, and interpret information in tables, including timetables
evidence: Read a bus timetable to find the departure time for a particular stop
Complete a two-way table from given data about favourite sports by gender
Calculate how long a train journey takes using a timetable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a timetable — like a train or bus timetable — to find out when a journey leaves, arrives, and how long it takes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical Analysis Vocabulary
topics.description: Read, write, and use the vocabulary of statistical analysis — mean, median, mode, range, frequency, data, sample, average, chart, table, graph, pie chart, scatter graph, correlation — with understanding of what each term describes
evidence: Correctly define and calculate the mean, median, mode, and range of a small data set
Use 'outlier' correctly to identify a value that doesn't fit the pattern, and explain its effect on the mean
Use 'correlation' correctly when describing the relationship shown in a scatter graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looked at a set of test scores from their class, could they find the mean, the median, and the range — and explain what each one tells you about how the class did?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating the Mean
topics.description: Calculate and interpret the mean as an average of a data set
evidence: Calculate the mean of five test scores: 72, 85, 90, 68, 95
Explain what the mean represents and how it differs from individual data values
Find a missing data value given the mean and all other values
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the family scored 6, 8, 7, 5, and 9 on a board game over five rounds, can {{name}} work out the mean (average) score?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line graphs
topics.description: Construct and interpret line graphs for continuous data (e.g. temperature over time, plant growth); read intermediate values, identify trends, and solve comparison and difference problems
evidence: Read values from a line graph showing temperature over a day, including estimating between plotted points
Construct a line graph from a table of continuous data, choosing an appropriate scale and labelling axes correctly
Use a line graph to solve a two-step problem, such as finding the time period with the greatest rate of change
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} recorded the temperature outside every hour for a day, could they plot those readings on a line graph with proper labels — and then use it to answer questions like 'when was it warmest?' or 'how much did it drop between 3pm and 6pm?'

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Line plots with fractions
topics.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); use operations on fractions to solve problems involving data in line plots (e.g. redistribute total equally)
evidence: Create a line plot showing lengths measured to the nearest 1/8 inch
Use the line plot to find the total of all measurements by adding fractions
Solve: 'If the total liquid were redistributed equally among all beakers, how much would each have?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured the lengths of several objects to the nearest quarter or eighth of an inch and plotted them on a number line, could they use those measurements to work out totals or share amounts equally?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pie charts
topics.description: Interpret and construct pie charts: calculate sector angles from data, draw sectors accurately, and read values from pie charts to solve problems
evidence: Read a pie chart and determine what fraction or percentage of the total each sector represents
Construct a pie chart from given data by calculating sector angles
Use a pie chart to determine the actual quantity represented by each sector given the total
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} read a pie chart — for example, one showing how a family spends its weekly budget — and use it to answer questions and solve problems?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Planning a statistical investigation
topics.description: Plan and conduct a statistical investigation by posing a question or identifying a problem, collecting relevant data, choosing appropriate displays, interpreting the data and communicating findings in context
evidence: Pose an investigation question such as 'Do Year 5 students sleep less on school nights?' and plan how to collect the data
Choose and justify a display (column graph, dot plot or table) for the collected data
Write a short report that answers the question and states one limitation of the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} come up with their own question — like whether kids sleep less on school nights — plan how to collect the data, and report what they found?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Validating and describing categorical data
topics.description: Acquire, validate and represent nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete numerical data using software including spreadsheets, process it (totals, differences), and report on the distribution by its mode and shape in context
evidence: Check a spreadsheet of survey responses for missing or impossible entries and correct or remove them
Classify 'favourite colour' as nominal and 'rating from 1 to 5' as ordinal and explain the difference
Use spreadsheet formulas to total each category, then report the mode and describe the shape of the column graph
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} collects survey answers in a spreadsheet, can they spot entries that don't make sense, total each category, and describe what the most common answer was?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Average distance from the mean
topics.description: Calculate the mean absolute deviation (MAD) of a small numerical data set — find the mean, find each value's distance from the mean (a non-negative number: a value equal to the mean has distance 0), then find the mean of those distances; interpret the MAD as the average distance of the values from the mean, stated in the original units of the data (e.g. minutes, cm, points); and use MADs to compare the spread or consistency of two data sets, recognising that a larger MAD means values typically sit further from the mean and that the MAD is 0 only when every value equals the mean
evidence: Calculate the MAD of 4, 6, 8, 9, 13 (mean 8; distances 4, 2, 0, 1, 5; MAD 2.4), counting the value equal to the mean as a distance of 0
Explain that a MAD of 3 cm for a set of plant heights means the heights are, on average, 3 cm away from the mean height
Decide which of two bowlers, both with a mean score of 120, is more consistent when their MADs are 8 and 21 points, and justify the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wrote down how many minutes late the school bus was each day for a week, could they work out how far each day was from the average lateness, average those distances, and explain what that number says about how reliable the bus is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Averages and range
topics.description: Describe, interpret, and compare observed distributions of a single variable using measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and spread (range), including choosing a suitable average and the effect of outliers; comparisons describe the observed data sets themselves and do not yet scale the difference in centres by a measure of variability or generalise from samples to wider populations
evidence: Find the mean, median and mode of 3, 5, 5, 6, 11 (6, 5 and 5) and say which average best represents a typical value
Find the range of 12, 14, 15, 15, 48 and explain why the outlier 48 pulls the mean (20.8) well above the median (15)
Compare two classes' spelling scores using their medians and ranges and write one conclusion about which class did better and one about which was more consistent
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} had the test scores of a whole class, could they find the mean, median, and range, and explain what each tells you about how the class performed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Box plots
topics.description: Construct and interpret a box plot on a numerical scale from a five-number summary (minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile, maximum), using the stated convention that the whiskers extend to the minimum and maximum values; interpret the median, quartiles, IQR and range, recognising that each whisker and each half of the box represents roughly a quarter of the data however long or short it is drawn; explain what a box plot does not show (individual values, clusters, gaps, the number of values, or the mean); and compare two distributions using their box plots
evidence: Draw a box plot for the five-number summary 3, 6, 9, 14, 21 on a labelled scale, stating that the whiskers run from the minimum to the maximum, and read the median, quartiles, IQR (8) and range (18) back from a given box plot

Explain that the longer upper whisker (from 14 to 21) shows the top quarter of values is more spread out — not that it contains more values — and reject claims a box plot cannot support, such as 'the mean is 9', 'most values are close to 9' or the exact number of data values

Explain with an example how two data sets can have the same box plot but different shapes (e.g. one with values spread evenly, the other with two clusters separated by a gap), and compare two classes' box plots using their medians and IQRs in context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees box plots comparing how long two classes spent on homework, could they say which class had the higher middle time and which was more spread out — and explain why a longer whisker doesn't mean more children are in that part?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing data sets digitally
topics.description: Interpret and compare data sets for nominal and ordinal categorical and discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays (side-by-side column graphs with ordinal categories in a common order, back-to-back dot plots) made with digital tools, processing the data (percentages, ranges) and comparing distributions by mode, range and shape
evidence: Make a side-by-side column graph in a spreadsheet comparing the favourite sports (nominal) of Year 3 and Year 6 students and state the mode for each group

Compare two classes' ratings of 'How much do you enjoy reading?' (never, sometimes, often, always) as percentages on side-by-side graphs with the categories in the same order, and say which class's ratings sit higher on the scale
Compare two classes' jump distances by mode, range and shape using back-to-back dot plots made with a digital tool
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has survey results from two classes of different sizes, can they use a spreadsheet to make a side-by-side graph, turn the counts into percentages, and compare the two fairly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Critiquing statistics in the media
topics.description: Identify statistically informed arguments in traditional and digital media and critique their methods, data representations (e.g. truncated axes, distorted pictographs, selective data) and conclusions
evidence: Explain how a bar graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 exaggerates a small difference
Identify the sample size and who was surveyed in a news claim such as '9 out of 10 kids prefer Brand X' and judge whether the conclusion is justified
Rewrite a misleading online headline so that it matches what the data actually show
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an ad saying '9 out of 10 kids prefer this cereal' or a graph with a stretched-out axis, can they ask who was asked and whether the graph makes the difference look bigger than it is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Describing distributions
topics.description: Describe the distribution of a numerical data set by its centre, spread and overall shape — recognising clusters, gaps, peaks, symmetry or skew (a longer tail on one side) and unusual values — and interpret each feature in the context in which the data were collected, recognising that distributions with similar centres can differ greatly in spread and shape
evidence: Describe a dot plot of 25 pupils' reaction times by its centre (a typical value), its spread (where most values lie and how far they extend) and its shape — naming any cluster, gap, symmetry or skew and unusual value — and link each feature to the context (e.g. a gap between two groups of times might reflect pupils who had practised and pupils who had not)

Compare two distributions with the same mean — e.g. two classes both averaging 60% on a test, one with scores clustered between 52% and 68%, the other spread from 20% to 95% in two separate clusters — and explain what the shared mean hides and why the difference matters in context

Use the context to judge whether an unusual value is more likely a recording error or a genuine extreme (e.g. a reaction time of 4.2 s among times near 0.3 s), and identify claims the display alone cannot support, such as the reason for a skew or that the same pattern would hold for a different group
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a dot plot of how long children in their class took to run 100 m, could they describe where most times bunch up, how spread out they are and whether there are any odd ones out — and suggest a sensible reason for what they see?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dot plots
topics.description: Construct and interpret dot plots for numerical data sets of any kind (counts, scores, times or measurements), extending earlier measurement line plots: draw a number-line scale with equal intervals that runs from at least the minimum to the maximum value, including values nobody recorded so that gaps stay visible; place one dot per observation, stacking repeated values in evenly spaced columns; label the scale with the attribute and its units; and read the plot to find how often a value occurs, the minimum, maximum and most common values, and the total number of observations, recognising that the height of a stack is a count of observations, not a data value
evidence: Draw a dot plot of 20 pupils' numbers of books read last month (values 0 to 12) on a scale marked 0, 1, 2, …, 12, leaving the empty value 7 visible as a gap and stacking the four 3s evenly
Read from a dot plot that the value 5 occurs 6 times, the minimum is 0, the maximum is 12 and the most common value is 5
Explain that a stack of 6 dots above 5 means six pupils each read 5 books, not that someone read 6 books, and count all the dots to give the number of pupils
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} asked 20 classmates how many books they read last month, could they draw a dot plot with one dot per person stacked above the right number on a number line — and then say how many classmates read exactly 5 books?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Histograms
topics.description: Construct and interpret histograms for continuous or numerical data grouped into equal-width class intervals on a continuous number-line scale, with no gaps between bars; state the interval-boundary convention used (e.g. 140 ≤ h < 150, so a value of exactly 150 belongs to the next interval); read frequencies from bar heights; describe the distribution shown; and explain how a histogram differs from a bar chart of categories. Unequal-width intervals and frequency density are not included.
evidence: Group 30 pupils' heights into equal-width 10 cm intervals (130 ≤ h < 140, 140 ≤ h < 150, …), stating that a height of exactly 150 cm is counted in the 150 ≤ h < 160 interval, and draw the histogram with a continuous horizontal scale, touching bars and labelled axes

Read frequencies accurately from a histogram (e.g. how many pupils are at least 150 cm but less than 160 cm, and how many are shorter than 150 cm in total) and describe the distribution's centre, spread and shape in context

Explain why a histogram's bars touch and sit on a numerical scale while a bar chart of categories (e.g. favourite sport) has gaps and an order that could be rearranged — and identify claims the histogram cannot support, such as the exact height of the tallest pupil or how many pupils are exactly 145 cm tall
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sorted the heights of everyone in their class into groups like '130 cm up to 140 cm' and '140 cm up to 150 cm', could they draw a histogram with the bars touching — and explain why it isn't the same kind of chart as a bar chart of favourite colours?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Pictograms and tally charts (age 11+)
topics.description: Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, and vertical line charts for both categorical and grouped numerical data, choosing appropriate representations for the data type
evidence: Construct a grouped frequency table from raw continuous data, choosing appropriate class intervals
Draw a pie chart by calculating the angle for each category
Interpret a bar chart comparing two data sets and draw a conclusion about the difference
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} collects data for a project, can they choose the right type of chart to display it — and draw it accurately with correct labels and a suitable scale?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Populations, samples and fair sampling
topics.description: Distinguish a population from a sample drawn from it; explain why a convenient or biased sample (choosing whoever is easiest to reach, volunteers, or a group linked to the answer) can misrepresent the population; explain that random selection gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen, which tends to produce representative samples — while recognising that any single random sample can still, by chance, be unrepresentative
evidence: In a described survey (e.g. a school asks 40 of its 800 pupils about the lunch menu), identify the population and the sample, and explain why a sample is used instead of asking everyone

Identify the selection bias in a sampling method (e.g. asking people leaving a gym how often they exercise, or surveying only the lunch queue on pizza day), explain the direction in which it would likely distort the result, and propose a better method using random selection from the whole population (e.g. drawing names from the full school register)

Explain the difference between random selection and simply choosing whoever is easiest to reach, and explain — with an example such as a random sample of 10 pupils that happens to contain mostly Year 7s — why random sampling makes a representative sample likely but does not guarantee it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a school wanted to know what all its pupils think of the lunch menu but only asked children in the lunch queue on pizza day, could {{name}} explain why that might give a misleading answer — and suggest a fairer way to choose who to ask, like picking names at random from the whole school list?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quartiles and interquartile range
topics.description: Find the median, lower quartile and upper quartile of a data set using one explicit convention — order the data, find the median, split the data into a lower and an upper half (leaving out the median itself when there is an odd number of values), and take the median of each half as the lower and upper quartile — while recognising that other textbooks, calculators and software may use slightly different conventions; calculate the interquartile range (IQR = upper quartile − lower quartile) and interpret it as the spread of the middle half of the data; and compare what the range and the IQR reveal, including their different sensitivity to extreme values
evidence: Using the stated convention, find the median (9), lower quartile (6, the median of 3, 5, 6, 7, 8) and upper quartile (14, the median of 11, 12, 14, 15, 21) of the 11 values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 21, giving IQR = 8; and for the 10 values 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, find median 7.5, lower quartile 4 and upper quartile 10, giving IQR = 6

Interpret an IQR in context (e.g. 'the middle half of the puzzle times lie between 6 and 14 minutes, a spread of 8 minutes') and explain that about half of the values lie between the quartiles, with about a quarter below the lower quartile and about a quarter above the upper quartile

Show that changing the largest value from 21 to 40 increases the range from 18 to 37 but leaves the IQR at 8, and use this to decide — and justify — whether the range or the IQR gives the better summary of spread for a data set with an extreme value or a long tail
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} lines up the times their friends took to finish a puzzle, could they find the middle time and the 'quarter-way' times either side of it — and explain why the gap between those quarter-way times is a better guide to how spread out most of the group is than the gap between the very fastest and slowest?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Refining a statistical investigation
topics.description: Plan and conduct a full statistical investigation by posing and refining questions or identifying a problem, planning and carrying out data collection, analysing and interpreting the data, and communicating findings in context
evidence: Refine a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into 'How many hours of organised sport do Year 6 students play each week?'
Plan and carry out the data collection, recording who was asked, how and when
Analyse the data with a suitable display and summary values and present a conclusion with one suggested improvement to the investigation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} turn a vague question like 'Do kids like sport?' into a precise one, collect the data, and present a conclusion with a suggestion for doing it better next time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Statistical questions
topics.description: Distinguish a statistical question — one that anticipates variability in the data collected to answer it, so its answer must account for that variability (even when it is reported as a single summary value such as a mean or median) — from a question answered by a single fixed fact; for a statistical question, identify the population (who or what is being asked about), the attribute being investigated, and the variation expected in the answers
evidence: Sort questions such as 'How tall am I?', 'How tall are the pupils in my class?', 'How many days are in March?' and 'How many hours of sleep do 12-year-olds usually get?' into statistical and non-statistical, explaining each choice by whether the answers are expected to vary

For a given statistical question, name the population and the attribute being measured, describe the variation they expect (e.g. 'sleep times will differ from person to person, perhaps from 7 to 11 hours'), and explain that a good answer must account for that variability in the data — even a single-number summary such as 'a typical 12-year-old sleeps about 9 hours' stands for many differing values, unlike the one fixed answer to 'How many days are in March?'

Explain why a question about a group can still be non-statistical (e.g. 'How many pupils are in my class?' has one fixed answer), and rewrite a non-statistical question as a statistical one (e.g. 'How long is my journey to school?' becomes 'How long are journeys to school for pupils in my year?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} whether 'How many pets does our family have?' and 'How many pets do children in your class have?' are the same kind of question, can they explain that the second one has lots of different answers — so you'd need to collect data from many people — while the first has just one answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What was measured, and how
topics.description: Before summarising a numerical data set, state its context precisely: report the number of observations (n) by counting the values in a list or the dots on a dot plot, or by adding the frequencies in a table or histogram (not by counting rows or bars); describe the attribute investigated (what was measured or counted, and for whom or what), how it was measured (the instrument or method and the precision or rounding used, e.g. measured with a tape to the nearest cm versus self-reported) and its units; and use these details to give every summary value with its units and to judge what the data can show, for example recognising when values bunch at round numbers because of how they were recorded
evidence: Report that a frequency table with frequencies 3, 7, 6 and 4 records 20 observations, not 4 (the number of rows) or 7 (the largest frequency)
Write a context statement such as 'hand spans of 28 pupils, measured with a ruler from thumb tip to little-finger tip, to the nearest 0.5 cm'
Explain that a pile-up of self-reported bedtimes at exactly 9:00 and 9:30 may come from people rounding their answers rather than from real bedtimes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measured classmates' hand spans for a project, could they say exactly how many people were measured, what was measured, how it was measured (e.g. with a ruler to the nearest half centimetre) and in what units — before giving any averages?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing a data summary
topics.description: Write a complete summary of a numerical data set in relation to its context, bringing together: the number of observations; the attribute, how it was measured and its units; a measure of centre with a matching measure of variability, each with units, chosen between median with IQR and mean with MAD; the overall pattern and any striking deviations, interpreted in context; and a justification of that choice by the shape of the distribution and the context (e.g. median and IQR for skewed data or data with extreme values, mean and MAD for roughly symmetric data without extreme values)
evidence: Write a summary of 25 pupils' reaction times that states n, the attribute, how it was measured and the units, a centre and a matching measure of spread with units, and any unusual value
Choose the median and IQR rather than the mean and MAD for a set of journey times with a long tail of slow journeys, and justify the choice by that tail
Rewrite the summary 'the average is 14' as 'the 30 pupils' median journey time is 14 minutes, with the middle half of times between 9 and 22 minutes'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} timed how long 25 friends took to solve a puzzle, could they write a short report saying how many were timed, how the times were measured, a typical time and how spread out the times were (with units) — and mention any time that stood out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing two populations
topics.description: Use measures of centre and variability calculated from random samples of two populations to make informal comparative inferences about those populations (e.g. whether words in a Grade 7 science book are generally longer than words in a Grade 4 science book): check that each sample was randomly drawn from the population it is meant to describe and is reasonably representative; weigh the difference between the sample centres against the variability within the samples and against how much centres vary from one random sample to another; and state qualified conclusions ('generally', 'on average', 'probably') rather than claiming every member of one population exceeds every member of the other — recognising that a small difference between two samples may be due to chance alone
evidence: Compare random samples of 20 word lengths from two books (means 6.2 and 4.4 letters, both MADs about 0.9) and conclude that the first book probably uses longer words on average
Explain why surveying volunteers at one school's sports club cannot support a conclusion that all pupils at that school are fitter than pupils at another school
Judge that a 1-point difference between two sample medians is not convincing when repeated random samples from one population give medians that vary by about 3 points
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} randomly picked 20 words from a Year 7 science book and 20 from a Year 4 science book, could they use the averages and spreads to decide whether the older book generally uses longer words — and explain why they'd say 'probably' rather than 'definitely'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating from a sample
topics.description: Use data from a random sample to estimate a characteristic of the population, such as a proportion, total count, or mean; present the result as an estimate rather than an exact population measurement; state the assumptions the inference relies on (the sample was randomly drawn from the population being described and is reasonably representative) and explain how the conclusion is limited or invalid when those assumptions fail
evidence: Use a sample proportion to estimate a population count — e.g. 18 of a random sample of 60 pupils walk to school, so estimate about 270 of the school's 900 pupils walk — and state the answer as an approximate estimate rather than an exact count

Use the mean of a random sample (e.g. the mean weekly reading time of 25 randomly chosen pupils) to estimate the population mean, and explain why the true population mean is likely to be close to, but probably not exactly equal to, the sample mean

State the assumptions behind an estimate and explain why it becomes unreliable or invalid when they fail — e.g. using a sample of only Year 7 pupils to estimate for the whole school, or using a volunteer online poll — and identify what can and cannot be concluded from the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} learns that 12 out of 40 randomly chosen pupils at their school play an instrument, could they estimate how many of the school's 600 pupils play one — and explain why that number is a sensible estimate rather than an exact count?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: How far apart two groups are
topics.description: Compare two numerical distributions with similar variability shown on a shared scale (e.g. dot plots) in two distinct ways: (1) judge their actual visual overlap directly from the displays — how much of each group's data lies among the other group's values; and (2) separately, find the difference between their centres and express it as a multiple of a clearly named measure of variability of either group, using matching measures (difference in means ÷ MAD, or difference in medians ÷ IQR), interpreting a larger multiple as centres that are further apart relative to the typical spread. Recognise that the same difference in centres means more when the variability is small, and that for similarly shaped, roughly symmetric, single-peaked distributions a larger multiple usually goes with less overlap — but that the ratio alone does not determine overlap: skew, clusters, gaps or outliers can make the visible overlap greater or smaller than the ratio suggests, so overlap is always checked on the display; and this simple ratio is only appropriate when the two variabilities are similar
evidence: Describe two dot plots of team heights drawn on the same scale as overlapping a lot, a little, or hardly at all, pointing to the range of heights the two teams share
Express a 10 cm difference in mean heights as about 2 MADs when each team's MAD is about 5 cm, naming MAD as the measure used
Use two dot plots whose means are 2 MADs apart, one with a long tail towards the other group, to explain why they overlap more than the 2-MAD gap alone would suggest
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the basketball team's average height is 10 cm more than the football team's, and players on each team are typically about 5 cm from their own team's average, could {{name}} explain that the gap is about twice the usual spread — and then look at a chart of both teams' heights to check how much they actually overlap, rather than guessing it from that number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: How samples vary
topics.description: Generate or compare several random samples of the same size from the same population (by drawing physically — returning and remixing the items before each new sample — from a list, or by simulation), observe that their estimates differ by chance, and use the spread of those estimates to judge how uncertain a single estimate or prediction is — distinguishing chance variation between random samples from the consistent error caused by a biased sampling method, and distinguishing variation between sample estimates from the variation among individual observations within a sample
evidence: Take or are given several random samples of the same size from one population (e.g. draw 20 counters from a bag without looking, record them, return all 20 and mix thoroughly, then draw the next 20 — five times; or five random samples of 20 names from a list), calculate each sample's proportion or mean, and show that the estimates differ

Explain that equal-sized random samples give different estimates because of chance in which individuals are selected, so a different result does not mean a sample was wrong — and contrast this with a biased method whose estimates are consistently too high or too low

Use the spread of several sample estimates (e.g. 'the estimates ranged from 25% to 40%') to say how far off a single estimate might be, and explain why one sample cannot make a prediction certain and why larger samples tend to give estimates that vary less

Distinguish the variation among individual observations within one sample (e.g. pupils' sleep times in one sample range from 6 to 11 hours) from the variation between sample estimates (e.g. the means of five samples of 20 pupils range from 8.6 to 9.3 hours), and explain why sample means usually vary much less than the individual values they are calculated from
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}}'s class takes turns drawing 20 sweets from the same big jar without looking — counting the red ones, then putting all 20 back and giving the jar a good shake before the next person draws — could {{name}} explain why each person gets a slightly different number of reds, and use the spread of everyone's results to say how sure they can be about the fraction of red sweets in the whole jar?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Finding halves and quarters (age 5+)
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a quarter as one of four equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into four equal parts and identify each as 'a quarter'
Find a quarter of 12 objects by sharing into 4 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into quarters (four equal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you fold a square piece of paper into four equal parts, can {{name}} tell you that each part is a quarter — and point to just one quarter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Is a Half?
topics.description: Recognise, find, and name a half as one of two equal parts of an object, shape, or quantity
evidence: Fold a shape into two equal parts and identify each as 'a half'
Find half of 8 objects by sharing into 2 equal groups
Identify whether a shape has been divided into halves or not (equal vs unequal parts)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is helping share a sandwich equally between two people, can they cut it so both pieces are the same size — and tell you each piece is called a half?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decomposing a shape into more equal shares
topics.description: Understand that decomposing a shape into more equal shares creates smaller shares
evidence: Explain that a quarter of a pizza is smaller than a half of the same pizza
Demonstrate that fourths are smaller pieces than halves
Compare the size of halves and quarters of the same shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pizza is shared between 2 people and then the same pizza is shared between 8 people, can {{name}} explain why each slice is smaller when more people share it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use fraction notation correctly — fraction, numerator, denominator, unit fraction, non-unit fraction, proper fraction, improper fraction, mixed number, equivalent fraction, simplest form — and understand what each term describes, including the roles of the numerator and denominator in expressing parts of a whole
evidence: Point to and name the numerator and denominator in any given fraction and explain what each tells you
Correctly classify fractions as unit, proper, improper, or mixed number with an example of each
Explain in own words why 2/4 and 1/2 are equivalent fractions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw the fraction 3/4 written down, could they point to the numerator and the denominator — and explain what each number actually means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts
topics.description: Recognise, find, name, and write fractions 1/3, 1/4, 2/4, and 3/4 of a length, shape, set of objects, or quantity
evidence: Find 1/3 of 12 objects by sharing into 3 equal groups
Shade 3/4 of a rectangle that has been divided into 4 equal parts
Identify 1/4 of a length on a number line or ruler
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you put 12 grapes on the table, can {{name}} count out a quarter of them — and then show you what three-quarters of the grapes looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves & Quarters of Shapes
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two and four equal shares and describe them using the words halves, fourths, and quarters
evidence: Divide a circle into two equal halves
Divide a rectangle into four equal quarters
Describe the whole as 'two halves' or 'four quarters'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a round pizza or a rectangular chocolate bar, can they divide it into four equal pieces and tell you each piece is called a quarter or a fourth?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Write simple fractions (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and recognise the equivalence of 2/4 and 1/2
evidence: Write 1/2 of 10 = 5
Explain that 2/4 is the same as 1/2 using a diagram
Calculate simple unit fractions of quantities and write the result
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 6 strawberries and eats half of them, can they write that as "1/2 of 6 = 3" — and explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same amount?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions
topics.description: Compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominator
evidence: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest
Explain that a larger denominator means smaller unit fractions
Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and explain that 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has eaten 3/8 of a cake and a friend has eaten 5/8 of the same cake, can they tell you who has eaten more — and put those fractions in order from smallest to biggest?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 7+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving counting in tenths, fractions of quantities, equivalence, fraction addition/subtraction, and fraction comparison
evidence: Solve a word problem requiring finding a fraction of a quantity
Solve a problem that requires comparing or ordering fractions
Choose and apply appropriate fraction knowledge to a multi-step problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bag of 20 sweets is shared equally among 5 friends, can {{name}} work out what fraction each person gets — and how many sweets that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions
topics.description: Recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
evidence: Show that 1/2 = 2/4 using a diagram of equal parts
Use a fraction wall or bar model to find equivalent fractions
Explain why two fractions are equivalent by comparing the shaded areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a bar divided into 4 equal parts with 2 shaded, can they tell you that's the same as 1/2 — and draw a different bar showing the same amount another way?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Recognise and use fractions as numbers: place unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators on a number line
evidence: Place 1/2, 1/4, 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 1
Identify that 1/3 lies between 0 and 1/2 on the number line
Understand that a fraction is a single number, not just 'part of a shape'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you draw a number line from 0 to 1, can {{name}} mark where 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4 should go — without any extra help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves, quarters and eighths
topics.description: Connect halves, quarters and eighths through repeated halving of shapes, objects and collections, and represent eighths of shapes and objects
evidence: Fold a paper strip in half, then half again, then half again, and label the halves, quarters and eighths
Show that 2 eighths of a pizza is the same amount as 1 quarter
Shade one-eighth of a square and one-eighth of a circle and explain how you know
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} keeps cutting a sandwich in half, then in half again, and again, can they name the pieces as halves, quarters and then eighths?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Simple Fraction Sums
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator within one whole (e.g. 5/7 + 1/7 = 6/7)
evidence: Calculate 2/5 + 2/5 = 4/5
Calculate 6/8 − 3/8 = 3/8
Explain that when denominators are the same, you add/subtract the numerators
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 2/8 of a cup of milk and then another 3/8 of a cup, can {{name}} work out the total without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Splitting shapes into equal parts (age 7+)
topics.description: Partition circles and rectangles into two, three, or four equal shares; describe shares as halves, thirds, and fourths; recognise that equal shares of identical wholes need not have the same shape
evidence: Partition a circle into 3 equal parts and label each 'a third'
Partition a rectangle into 4 equal shares in more than one way
Explain that two different-looking shares can still be equal in size
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a rectangle into thirds in two different ways (three strips vs three squares), can {{name}} recognise that both give equal thirds — even though the pieces look different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths
topics.description: Count up and down in tenths; recognise that tenths arise from dividing an object into 10 equal parts and from dividing one-digit numbers or quantities by 10
evidence: Count: one tenth, two tenths, three tenths … up to ten tenths (one whole)
Show that dividing a shape into 10 equal parts gives tenths
Explain that 3 ÷ 10 = 3/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} splits a chocolate bar with 10 equal pieces, can they tell you each piece is one tenth — and count up from 1/10 to 10/10 in order?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unit fractions
topics.description: Recognise, find, and write fractions of a discrete set of objects: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
evidence: Find 1/4 of 12 objects by dividing into 4 equal groups
Find 3/4 of 12 objects
Write the fraction of a set that is shaded or selected
topics.assessmentPrompt: If there are 15 books on a shelf, can {{name}} work out how many two-thirds of them is — and check by grouping the books into three equal piles?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding Fractions (Same Denominator)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with the same denominator, including results greater than one whole (e.g. 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8)
evidence: Calculate 3/5 + 4/5 = 7/5 and explain it equals 1 2/5
Subtract 2/6 from 5/6
Solve addition problems where the sum exceeds the whole: 7/8 + 3/8
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe uses 5/8 of a bag of flour and then another 6/8, can {{name}} work out the total and explain what the answer means as a mixed number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare two fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator by reasoning about size; record comparisons with >, =, or < symbols
evidence: Compare 3/8 and 3/4: same numerator, larger denominator means smaller pieces so 3/8 < 3/4
Compare 5/6 and 2/6: same denominator so 5/6 > 2/6
Justify a comparison using a visual model and explain why both fractions must refer to the same whole
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 3/5 and 3/8, can they tell you which is bigger just by thinking about the size of each piece — without needing to draw it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal equivalents of tenths and hundredths
topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of any number of tenths or hundredths (e.g. 3/10 = 0.3, 27/100 = 0.27)
evidence: Write 7/10 as 0.7 and vice versa
Convert 45/100 to 0.45
Place 0.3 and 3/10 at the same point on a number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 7/10 on a price label, can they rewrite it as a decimal — and do the same thing for 43/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal & Percent Notation
topics.description: Read, write, and use decimal and percentage notation correctly — decimal, decimal point, tenths, hundredths, thousandths, percentage, per cent, % symbol, convert, terminating decimal — and understand the relationships between fractions, decimals, and percentages as three ways of expressing the same value
evidence: Read and write decimal numbers correctly, identifying the value of each digit (ones, tenths, hundredths)
Use the % symbol correctly and explain that per cent means 'out of 100'
Convert between simple fractions, decimals, and percentages (e.g. 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%) and explain why they are equal
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} saw '0.5' and '50%' written down, could they explain that they both mean the same amount — and write them as a fraction too?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Round decimals with one decimal place to the nearest whole number
evidence: Round 3.7 to 4 and 3.2 to 3
Place 6.5 on a number line between 6 and 7 and decide it rounds to 7
Round a set of one-decimal-place numbers and explain the rounding rule
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures something as 3.7 m, can they tell you whether that rounds to 3 m or 4 m — and explain why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value (age 8+)
topics.description: Compare numbers with the same number of decimal places up to two decimal places
evidence: Order 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 from smallest to largest
Compare 3.72 and 3.27 using place-value reasoning
Place three two-decimal-place numbers on a number line in order
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing two prices — £4.75 and £4.57 — can they tell you which is more expensive without using a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimals and fractions
topics.description: Solve simple measure and money problems involving fractions and decimals to two decimal places
evidence: Calculate 1/4 of £3.20
A rope is 2.5 m long; how much is left after cutting 0.75 m?
Find 3/10 of 1 kg and express the answer in grams and as a decimal of a kg
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a bottle holds 1.5 litres and {{name}} drinks 0.75 litres, can they work out how much is left — and write it as both a decimal and a fraction?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by 10 and 100
topics.description: Find the effect of dividing a one- or two-digit number by 10 and 100, identifying the value of the digits as ones, tenths, and hundredths
evidence: Calculate 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 and identify 3 as ones and 7 as tenths
Calculate 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 and identify 4 as hundredths
Explain that dividing by 10 shifts each digit one place to the right
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts with the number 48 and divides it by 10, can they tell you the answer — and explain what happened to each digit's place value?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate simple equivalent fractions and explain why they are equivalent using visual fraction models
evidence: Given 1/3, generate 2/6 as equivalent and show with area model
Simplify 4/8 to 1/2 and justify with a fraction strip
Complete equivalence chains: 1/4 = ?/8 = ?/12
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is shown a fraction bar split into 3 parts with 1 shaded (= 1/3), can they draw an equivalent bar with 6 parts that shows exactly the same amount shaded?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Equivalent fractions on a number line
topics.description: Understand two fractions as equivalent if they are the same size or the same point on a number line; recognise and show families of common equivalent fractions using diagrams
evidence: Use fraction strips to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6
Verify on a number line that 2/3 and 4/6 land on the same point
Identify at least three fractions equivalent to 1/2 using diagrams
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees that 2/4 and 1/2 land on the exact same point on a number line, can they explain in their own words why those two fractions are equal?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fraction-Decimal Equivalents
topics.description: Recognise and write decimal equivalents of 1/4, 1/2, and 3/4
evidence: Match fractions to decimals in a sorting activity
Explain why 1/4 = 25/100 = 0.25 using a hundredths grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 3/4 of a cup of flour, can {{name}} tell you what that is as a decimal — without looking it up?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions as parts of shapes
topics.description: Partition shapes into parts with equal areas and express the area of each part as a unit fraction of the whole
evidence: Partition a rectangle into 6 equal-area parts and label each 1/6
Show two different ways to partition a square into 4 equal parts
Given a pre-partitioned shape, write the unit fraction for one part
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to fold a square piece of paper into 8 equal parts, can they tell you what fraction of the whole square each part represents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of amounts (harder)
topics.description: Solve problems involving increasingly harder fractions to calculate quantities, including non-unit fractions where the answer is a whole number
evidence: Find 3/5 of 20
Calculate 2/3 of 18 and explain the two-step process (divide then multiply)
Solve: A bag has 24 sweets, 3/8 are red — how many red sweets?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If 3/4 of a class of 28 pupils brought their homework in, can {{name}} work out exactly how many pupils that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole
topics.description: Understand a fraction 1/b as the quantity formed by 1 part when a whole is partitioned into b equal parts; understand a/b as a parts of size 1/b
evidence: Given a shape divided into 5 equal parts, identify one shaded part as 1/5
Explain that 3/4 means 3 parts each of size 1/4
Draw a model showing 2/6 as 2 pieces of a whole cut into 6
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you cut a pizza into 6 equal slices, can {{name}} explain what 1/6 means — and then work out what 4/6 of the pizza looks like?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of a whole (age 8+)
topics.description: Express whole numbers as fractions (e.g. 3 = 3/1) and recognise fractions equivalent to whole numbers (e.g. 4/4 = 1, 6/1 = 6)
evidence: Write 5 as 5/1 and explain why
Locate 4/4 and 1 at the same point on a number line
Identify which fractions from a list equal a whole number: 6/3, 8/4, 5/2
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} to write the number 3 as a fraction, can they write 3/1 — and also tell you what fraction equals exactly 1 whole, like 4/4 or 5/5?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line (age 8+)
topics.description: Represent fractions on a number line: partition the interval 0 to 1 into b equal parts to locate 1/b, then mark off a lengths of 1/b from 0 to locate a/b
evidence: Partition a 0-to-1 number line into 4 equal parts and mark 1/4
Explain that each part on the line has size 1/b
Locate 1/3 and 1/6 on separate number lines
Locate 3/4 on a number line by counting three 1/4-jumps from 0
Place 5/6 on a number line and explain the process
Identify a fraction shown by a point on a pre-partitioned number line
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a number line from 0 to 1 split into 5 equal parts, can they label where 2/5 and 4/5 go — and explain how they worked it out?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Tenths (age 8+)
topics.description: Count up and down in hundredths; recognise that hundredths arise when dividing an object by 100 or dividing tenths by 10
evidence: Count from 3/100 to 12/100 in hundredths
Explain that 1/10 ÷ 10 = 1/100
Place several hundredths on a number line between 0 and 1/10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has £1 and spends 37p, can they say that 37p is 37/100 of a pound — and count up in hundredths from 0/100 to 100/100?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding and subtracting mixed numbers
topics.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, including by converting to improper fractions or using properties of operations
evidence: Calculate 2 3/5 + 1 4/5 and express as a mixed number
Subtract 3 1/4 from 5 3/4
Solve 4 2/6 − 1 5/6 by regrouping the whole number
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe calls for 1 and 2/5 cups of oats and another batch needs 2 and 3/5 cups, can {{name}} add them together to get the total — including converting when the fifths add up past a whole?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Adding fractions (different denominators)
topics.description: Add and subtract fractions with denominators that are multiples of the same number by finding a common denominator
evidence: Calculate 1/3 + 1/6 by converting to sixths: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2
Calculate 3/4 − 1/8 by converting to eighths
Add 2/5 + 3/10 and simplify the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to add 1/3 and 1/6, can they find a common denominator and work out the total — showing their working?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Addition and subtraction word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions with like denominators, using visual models and equations
evidence: A jug contains 3/4 litre of juice; 2/4 litre is poured out — how much remains?
Two pieces of ribbon are 2 3/8 and 1 5/8 inches — what is their total length?
Draw a fraction model to represent and solve a fraction word problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads that one section of a nature trail is 3/8 km and another is 5/8 km, can they work out the total distance without a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Decimals
topics.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths (or up to three decimal places) by reasoning about size using place-value understanding; record with >, =, <
evidence: Compare 0.45 and 0.405 and explain which is greater
Order 3.142, 3.14, 3.2 from smallest to largest
Justify that 0.7 = 0.70 = 0.700 using place-value reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} compares 0.45 and 0.54, can they use place value to explain which is bigger — without reaching for a calculator?

topics.subject: Mathematics
