topics.description: Solve word problems involving lengths within 100, using addition and subtraction with drawings and equations
evidence: Solve 'The rope is 45 cm long. I cut off 18 cm. How long is it now?'
Draw a diagram (e.g. a ruler drawing) to represent a length word problem
Write an equation with a symbol for the unknown to represent the problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a piece of rope 75 cm long and cuts off 28 cm, can they work out how much rope is left — and draw a number-line diagram to show it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: a.m. and p.m. times
topics.description: Tell and write times to five minutes on analogue and digital clocks with a.m. or p.m. (before or after midday), relating times to daily events and using the words morning, afternoon, evening, noon and midnight. Roman-numeral clock faces and the 24-hour clock are covered in Roman numeral and 24-hour clocks
evidence: Say whether school starts at 8:45 a.m. or 8:45 p.m., and whether bedtime is 7:30 a.m. or 7:30 p.m.
Write 'twenty-five past four in the afternoon' as 4:25 p.m.
Explain that 12 noon is midday, so times just after it are p.m., while times just after midnight are a.m.
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a clock shows 7:45, can {{name}} tell you the time in words — and say whether breakfast would be at 7:45 a.m. or 7:45 p.m.?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculating with measurements
topics.description: Measure, compare, add, and subtract lengths (m/cm/mm), mass (kg/g), and volume/capacity (l/ml) using standard units
evidence: Measure a length in centimetres and millimetres
Weigh an object using grams and kilograms
Add two measurements in the same unit (e.g. 250 ml + 400 ml = 650 ml)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} pours 350 ml into a jug and then adds another 275 ml, can they work out the total — and tell you how much more is needed to reach 1 litre?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing lengths by measuring
topics.description: Measure to determine how much longer one object is than another, expressing the length difference in terms of a standard length unit
evidence: Measure two objects and calculate the difference in length
Express the difference using the correct unit (e.g. '7 cm longer')
Solve a comparison problem: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a pencil is 16 cm and a crayon is 9 cm, can {{name}} work out how much longer the pencil is — without measuring them side by side?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Comparing Time Durations
topics.description: Compare durations of events and calculate the time taken by particular events or tasks
evidence: Work out that a TV show from 5:17 p.m. to 5:43 p.m. lasted 26 minutes
Compare a 35-minute bus journey with a 40-minute walk and say which takes longer and by how much
Solve 'The lesson starts at 10:15 and ends at 11:00. How long is it?' (45 minutes)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts cooking at 4:15 p.m. and finishes at 5:00 p.m., can they work out how long the cooking took?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating Lengths
topics.description: Estimate lengths using units of inches, feet, centimetres, and metres
evidence: Estimate the length of a classroom object before measuring it
Use a known reference (e.g. width of a finger ≈ 1 cm) to make reasonable estimates
Check estimates by measuring and evaluate how close they were
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a car parked outside, can they estimate roughly how many metres long it is — and then check whether their guess was reasonable?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions of time and events
topics.description: Identify common uses of halves, quarters and eighths in relation to events and time, such as half-time in a game, half an hour, a quarter of an hour, and an activity split into eight equal time parts
evidence: Describe half-time in a football game as the point when half the playing time is over, and explain that half an hour is 30 minutes because an hour is split into 2 equal parts
Show a quarter of an hour on a clock face as a quarter of the way round
Represent a 16-minute class activity as a strip of eight equal 2-minute parts, colour one part and say it is one eighth of the activity (2 minutes)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a 16-minute game is split into 8 equal turns, can {{name}} work out that each turn is one eighth of the game — 2 minutes — and do they know that half an hour is 30 minutes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Giving Change
topics.description: Add and subtract amounts of money to give change, using both £ and p in practical contexts
evidence: Calculate the total cost of two or three items priced in pounds and pence
Work out the change from £5 or £10
Record money calculations using £ and p notation correctly (e.g. £3.47)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} buys a book for £3.50 and a pencil for £1.25 with a £5 note, can they work out exactly how much change they should receive?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring length (age 7+)
topics.description: Measure the length of an object by selecting and using appropriate tools such as rulers, yardsticks, metre sticks, and measuring tapes
evidence: Choose the most appropriate tool for measuring a given object
Align the zero mark of a ruler with the end of the object and read the measurement
Measure lengths in inches, feet, centimetres, and metres using the correct tool
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to measure a piece of fabric about 80 cm long, can they pick the right tool — a short ruler or a tape measure — and use it accurately?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Perimeters
topics.description: Measure the perimeter of simple 2-D shapes
evidence: Measure each side of a rectangle and add the lengths to find the perimeter
Calculate the perimeter of a regular shape given the side length
Explain that perimeter is the total distance around a shape
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to put a decorative border around a rectangular picture frame 20 cm wide and 30 cm tall, can they work out the total length of border needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring & Plotting Lengths
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest whole unit and display the data on a line plot
evidence: Measure the lengths of several objects and record the data
Create a line plot with a horizontal scale marked in whole-number units
Interpret a line plot to answer questions about the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the length of ten leaves to the nearest cm and records the results, can they display the data on a simple number-line plot — grouping leaves of the same length?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring with different units
topics.description: Measure the length of an object using two different length units and describe how the measurements relate to the size of the unit chosen
evidence: Measure a desk in both centimetres and inches and compare the two numbers
Explain that measuring with a smaller unit gives a larger number
Predict whether a measurement in centimetres will be greater or less than in inches
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures the same book in centimetres and then in inches, can they explain why the numbers are different even though the book hasn't changed size?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money transactions in dollars
topics.description: Solve practical money transactions with Australian money involving addition, subtraction and equal groups — totals, change and costs of several identical items — and explain the answer in terms of the purchase
evidence: Work out the total cost of a $4 drink and a $7 sandwich and the change from a $20 note
Find the cost of 3 apples at 50c each by repeated addition
Make 85c using the fewest Australian coins and explain the choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: At the canteen, if {{name}} buys a $4 drink and a $7 sandwich with a $20 note, can they work out how much change they should get?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Money word problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving dollar bills, quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies, using $ and ¢ symbols appropriately
evidence: Determine the total value of a collection of coins
Solve a word problem about making change with US currency
Use $ and ¢ symbols correctly in answers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 2 quarters, 1 dime, and 3 pennies, can they work out the total — and tell you whether that's enough to buy something costing 65 cents?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Quarter past and quarter to
topics.description: Recognise, read and show quarter past and quarter to the hour on an analog clock, linking each to a quarter turn of the minute hand
evidence: Read a clock showing 3:15 as 'quarter past three'
Set the hands of a clock to quarter to seven
Explain that the minute hand has turned a quarter of the way round at quarter past
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at an analog clock and the big hand points to the 3, can they say it's 'quarter past'? And can they recognise 'quarter to' when it points to the 9?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Roman numeral and 24-hour clocks
topics.description: Tell and write the time from analogue clocks with Roman-numeral faces (I to XII, including IV, which some clocks show as IIII, and IX), knowing that the minute positions are the same as on a clock with ordinary numbers; and read and write times on 12-hour and 24-hour clocks, knowing that the 24-hour clock runs from 00:00 at midnight to 23:59. Times from 1:00 a.m. to 11:59 a.m. keep the same hour (7:05 a.m. = 07:05); times from 1:00 p.m. to 11:59 p.m. are 12 hours more (3:20 p.m. = 15:20). The 12 o'clock hour is the exception to both: 12:20 p.m., just after noon, stays 12:20, and 12:20 a.m., just after midnight, becomes 00:20. Fluent conversion between 12- and 24-hour times is developed in Year 4
evidence: Read a Roman-numeral clock with the minute hand on IX and the hour hand between IV and V as quarter to five (4:45)
Match the Roman numerals I to XII to the hour positions on a blank clock face, including IV (or IIII), IX and XII
Write 3:20 p.m. as 15:20 and 7:05 a.m. as 07:05, then write 12:20 p.m. as 12:20 and 12:20 a.m. as 00:20, explaining why adding 12 works only for p.m. times from 1 p.m. onwards
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees a clock with Roman numerals where the minute hand points to IX and the hour hand is between IV and V, can they read it as quarter to five — and say what time 15:20 on a 24-hour clock means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Smaller units for accuracy
topics.description: Choose a smaller uniform informal unit when a measurement needs to be more accurate, recognising that a smaller unit gives a larger count, for length, mass and capacity
evidence: Measure a book with pencils (about 2) and then with paperclips (about 9) and explain why the paperclip count is bigger
Choose teaspoons instead of cups to measure how much a small glass holds and explain why
Explain why '3 and a bit hand spans' is less accurate than measuring the same table in counting cubes
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures a book with pencils and gets 'about 2', can they see that using smaller paperclips would give a more exact measurement — and a bigger number?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time to the nearest minute
topics.description: Tell, write and estimate the time to the nearest minute on analogue and digital clocks, using vocabulary such as o'clock, a.m./p.m., morning, afternoon, noon and midnight; record and compare times and durations in seconds, minutes and hours
evidence: Read 7:43 from an analogue clock face and write it on a digital display
Estimate whether brushing teeth takes about 2 seconds, 2 minutes or 2 hours, then time it to check
Compare 1 minute 20 seconds with 75 seconds and say which is longer
topics.assessmentPrompt: If the kitchen clock shows 7:43, can {{name}} read the exact time and write it as it would look on a digital clock — and say which is longer, 1 minute 20 seconds or 75 seconds?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Time Units and Calendar Facts
topics.description: Know the number of seconds in a minute and the number of days in each month, year, and leap year
evidence: State that there are 60 seconds in a minute
Name the months and state the number of days in each
Explain that a leap year has 366 days and occurs every 4 years
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you ask {{name}} how many days are in September and whether this year is a leap year, can they answer both — and tell you how many seconds are in a minute?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Using a calendar
topics.description: Read a calendar to identify today's date and the day of the week for a given date, and determine the number of days between two events
evidence: Find 15 March on a calendar page and say which day of the week it is
Write today's date from the classroom calendar in day-month form
Count how many days from 3 June to a birthday on 17 June
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at the family calendar, can they find today's date and count how many days are left until their birthday or the school holidays?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: 12-hour and 24-hour time
topics.description: Read, write, and convert time between analogue and digital 12-hour and 24-hour clocks
evidence: Convert 3:45 pm to 15:45 in 24-hour time
Read 19:30 and state the 12-hour equivalent as 7:30 pm
Match a set of 12-hour and 24-hour times
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a train timetable shows a departure at 14:35, can {{name}} convert that to 12-hour clock time — and tell you whether that's morning or afternoon?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area (age 8+)
topics.description: Measure areas by counting unit squares (square cm, square m, square in, square ft)
evidence: Count unit squares to find the area of an L-shaped figure
Measure the area of a book cover using square-centimetre tiles
Compare areas of two shapes by counting their unit squares
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} draws a shape on squared centimetre paper, can they find its area by counting the squares — including making a sensible estimate for any partial squares?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and the distributive property
topics.description: Use tiling to demonstrate the distributive property: the area of a rectangle with sides a and (b+c) equals a×b + a×c; use area models to represent the distributive property
evidence: Tile a 3×(4+2) rectangle and show it decomposes into 3×4 and 3×2
Use an area model to compute 6×13 as 6×10 + 6×3
Draw an area model showing 5×(7+3) = 5×7 + 5×3
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to work out 6 × 13 by splitting it into 6 × 10 and 6 × 3, can they draw a rectangle divided into two parts to show why that method works?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area by Tiling
topics.description: Find the area of a rectangle by tiling it with unit squares and show that the result equals the product of the side lengths
evidence: Tile a 4×6 rectangle and count 24 squares, then verify 4×6=24
Explain why the number of rows times the number in each row gives the area
Draw a rectangle on squared paper, tile it, and write the multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a rectangular room is 4 m long and 3 m wide, can {{name}} work out its area by tiling it with 1-metre squares in their head — and explain why that equals 4 × 3?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of compound shapes
topics.description: Recognise area as additive; find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing into non-overlapping rectangles and summing their areas
evidence: Decompose an L-shape into two rectangles, find each area, and add them
Find the area of a floor plan shaped like a T by splitting into rectangles
Solve: A room is L-shaped (3m×5m plus 2m×4m) — what is the total area?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped room on squared paper, can they split it into two rectangles, find the area of each part, and add them to get the total area?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of rectangles by multiplication
topics.description: Multiply side lengths to find areas of rectangles and represent whole-number products as rectangular areas
evidence: Calculate the area of a 7 cm × 9 cm rectangle as 63 cm²
Draw a rectangle with area 36 square units and label its side lengths
Solve: A garden is 8 m by 5 m — what is its area?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to carpet a room that is 5 m by 4 m, can they work out how much carpet to buy — using multiplication rather than counting squares?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting measurement units
topics.description: Convert between different units of measure (e.g. kilometre to metre, hour to minute, minute to second, year to month, week to day)
evidence: Convert 3 km to 3000 m
State 2 hours = 120 minutes
Convert 5 weeks to 35 days
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told a journey is 3.5 km, can they convert that to metres — and also turn 2 hours 15 minutes into just minutes?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dollars and cents
topics.description: Recognise the relationship between dollars and cents (100 cents = 1 dollar), read and write amounts in $ and c notation (e.g. $3.45 and 345c), represent the same amount with different combinations of Australian coins and notes, and calculate change in dollars and cents
evidence: Write $2.70 as 270c and 450c as $4.50
Show $3.60 in two different ways using Australian coins and notes
Work out the change from a $10 note for a purchase costing $6.40
topics.assessmentPrompt: At the shops, can {{name}} read a price like $3.45, explain that it means 3 dollars and 45 cents, and work out the change from a $10 note?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Elapsed time problems
topics.description: Solve word problems involving elapsed time by adding and subtracting time intervals in minutes, including using a number line
evidence: A film starts at 2:15 and lasts 47 minutes — when does it end?
Calculate how many minutes between 9:20 and 10:05
Use a number line to show the elapsed time between two events
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} starts football practice at 3:20 p.m. and it lasts 75 minutes, can they work out what time it finishes — using a number line to help?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating and comparing money
topics.description: Estimate, compare, and calculate different measures including money in pounds and pence
evidence: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres
Compare 1.5 kg and 1200 g and identify which is heavier
Calculate the total cost of 3 items at £2.45, £1.30, and £0.75
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is comparing three items costing £2.85, £3.10, and £2.50, can they put them in order from cheapest to most expensive — and work out the total cost?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Halves and quarters (age 8+)
topics.description: Generate measurement data by measuring lengths to the nearest half and quarter inch; display the data on a line plot with a scale marked in whole numbers, halves, and quarters
evidence: Measure five objects to the nearest 1/4 inch
Create a line plot showing the lengths of classmates' pencils in half-inches
Read a line plot and answer questions about the data
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} measures ten pencil lengths to the nearest quarter inch, can they record the data and plot it on a number line split into quarters — then spot which length appears most?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measuring Liquids & Masses
topics.description: Measure and estimate liquid volumes and masses of objects using grams, kilograms, and litres; solve one-step word problems involving mass or volume
evidence: Estimate the mass of a textbook in grams or kilograms
Read a scale to measure liquid volume in litres
Solve: 3 bags weigh 250 g each — what is the total mass?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling bottles that each hold 250 ml from a 2-litre container of juice, can they work out how many bottles they can fill?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeters of polygons
topics.description: Solve problems involving perimeters of polygons: find perimeter from side lengths, find an unknown side length, and explore rectangles with same perimeter but different areas (or vice versa)
evidence: Calculate the perimeter of a rectangle with sides 8 cm and 5 cm
Find the missing side of a pentagon with perimeter 30 cm and four known sides
Draw two rectangles both with perimeter 24 cm but different areas
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm and one side is 8 cm, can {{name}} work out the length of the other side — without drawing it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding Area
topics.description: Understand that a unit square has one square unit of area and that the area of a plane figure is the number of unit squares that cover it without gaps or overlaps
evidence: Identify a unit square and state its area is 1 square unit
Explain why a figure covered by 12 unit squares has area 12 square units
Distinguish between area and perimeter as different measurements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} counts the small squares inside a rectangle drawn on squared paper, can they tell you the area — and explain what "one square unit" means?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area and perimeter of rectangles
topics.description: Apply the area formula (l × w) and perimeter formula (2l + 2w) for rectangles including squares in real-world and mathematical problems; calculate and compare areas using standard units (cm², m²) and estimate areas of irregular shapes
evidence: Find the width of a room given area = 48 m² and length = 8 m
Calculate the area of a square with side 7.5 cm
Estimate the area of an irregular pond drawn on a cm² grid
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to carpet a room 6.5 m × 4 m, can they calculate the area — and also work out how many metres of skirting board are needed around the edge?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Converting measurement units (age 9+)
topics.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system (km/m/cm/mm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min/sec); convert between different metric units and express measurements in terms of a smaller unit; record equivalents in conversion tables
evidence: Convert 3.5 km to 3,500 m
Complete a conversion table for cm and mm: (1,10), (2,20), (3,30)...
Express 2 kg 350 g as 2,350 g
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 3.5 kg to grams, can they do it confidently — and also fill in a simple two-column table showing the same measurements in kg and g?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Counting Unit Cubes
topics.description: Measure and estimate the volume of solids by counting unit cubes: build cuboids from 1 cm³ cubes and count them, count the cubes in models and drawings (including hidden cubes), estimate how many cubes will fill a box and check by filling it, and record volumes in cubic units (cm³, in³, ft³ or improvised units)
evidence: Build a 3 × 2 × 2 cuboid from 1 cm³ cubes and state its volume as 12 cm³
Count the cubes in a drawing of a solid built from cubes, including the hidden ones at the back, and give the volume in cubic units
Estimate how many centimetre cubes will fill a small box, then fill it to check
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a small cardboard box, can they estimate how many sugar cubes would fit inside and then fill it to check — and count the cubes in a picture of a cube model, including the hidden ones at the back?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating capacity
topics.description: Estimate the capacity of containers in litres and millilitres by comparing them with known measures (e.g. a 1-litre bottle) and check by filling with water; distinguish a container's capacity (how much it can hold) from the volume of liquid in it. Estimating the volume of solids with 1 cm³ cubes is covered in Counting Unit Cubes
evidence: Estimate whether a mug holds about 30 ml, 300 ml or 3 litres, then check with a measuring jug
Estimate the capacity of a jug by comparing it with a 1-litre bottle, then fill it with water to check
Explain that a 1-litre jug half full of water has a capacity of 1 litre but holds 500 ml of water
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} looks at a saucepan, can they estimate whether it holds about half a litre, 2 litres or 10 litres — and check by filling it with water from a 1-litre jug?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating money totals
topics.description: Use estimation and rounding to check and explain the reasonableness of money calculations in dollars and cents, including rounding cash totals to the nearest 5 cents as Australian shops do, and solve practical financial problems
evidence: Estimate the total of $4.95, $2.10 and $7.85 as about $15 before calculating the exact total
Round a cash total of $12.37 to $12.35 and $8.48 to $8.50 and explain the 5-cent rule
Decide whether $36 change from $50 is reasonable after buying items costing $6.90 and $8.15
topics.assessmentPrompt: At the supermarket, can {{name}} round the prices in the trolley to estimate the total before you pay — and tell whether the change you get back looks about right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fractions on a number line
topics.description: Solve word problems involving distances, time intervals, liquid volumes, masses, and money using the four operations with fractions or decimals; represent with diagrams including number lines
evidence: A 2.5 kg bag of flour is split equally into 4 portions — what does each weigh?
A journey takes 1 hr 45 min; what time do you arrive if you leave at 09:20?
Three ribbons of 0.75 m, 1.2 m, and 0.95 m — what is the total length?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is planning a 4.5 km walk and has already walked 1.75 km, can they work out how far is left — and estimate how long the remaining walk might take?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement Line Plots
topics.description: Make a line plot to display measurement data in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8); solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions using line plot data
evidence: Create a line plot of seed growth measurements in 1/8-inch increments
Use a line plot to find the difference between the longest and shortest specimens
Calculate the total length of all items in a line plot by adding the fractional measurements
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} records caterpillar lengths as fractions of an inch and plots them on a number line, can they work out the total length of three caterpillars by adding the fractions from the plot?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Metric & Imperial Conversion
topics.description: Understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units (inches, pounds, pints)
evidence: State that 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm and use this to estimate length in inches
Know that 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds and estimate a person's weight in pounds
Convert approximately between litres and pints (1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} hears that a baby weighs 7 pounds, can they give a rough idea of that in kilograms — using the approximate conversion they know?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter of Compound Shapes
topics.description: Measure and calculate the perimeter of composite rectilinear shapes in centimetres and metres
evidence: Find the perimeter of an L-shaped figure by identifying all side lengths
Calculate the perimeter of a composite shape where some sides must be deduced
Draw a composite rectilinear shape with a perimeter of 40 cm
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given an L-shaped garden plan with all the side measurements labelled, can they add all the sides together to find the total perimeter?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading between scale marks
topics.description: Interpret unmarked and partial units on scaled instruments and read digital instruments when measuring length, mass, capacity, duration and temperature, using appropriate units
evidence: Read 500 g on kitchen scales numbered every 200 g where the pointer sits halfway between 400 g and 600 g
Read 175 ml on a jug marked every 50 ml and 23 degrees on a thermometer marked every 2 degrees
Read and record a time of 1 minute 26.4 seconds from a digital stopwatch and a length of 12.7 cm on a ruler
topics.assessmentPrompt: When {{name}} helps with baking, can they read the scales when the pointer is between two numbers — like halfway between 400 g and 600 g?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Telling time to the minute (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving converting between units of time (hours↔minutes, minutes↔seconds, years↔months, weeks↔days)
evidence: Convert 3 hours 25 minutes to 205 minutes
A programme lasts 150 seconds — express in minutes and seconds
How many days are in 8 weeks and 3 days?
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 2 hours 35 minutes into just minutes, can they do it — and then convert 180 seconds into minutes and seconds?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What volume means
topics.description: Recognise volume as an attribute of solid figures; understand that a unit cube (side length 1 unit) has 'one cubic unit' of volume and can be used to measure volume; a solid packed with n unit cubes has volume n cubic units
evidence: Explain what 'volume' means for a 3D shape and how it differs from area
Identify a unit cube and explain that it represents one cubic unit of volume
Determine the volume of a small solid by counting the unit cubes that fill it
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} builds a solid shape using small cubes, can they count the cubes to find the volume — and explain what "one cubic centimetre" means in everyday terms?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area of Triangles & Parallelograms
topics.description: Find the area of parallelograms and triangles by relating them to rectangles: rearrange a parallelogram (cut off a triangle and move it) into a rectangle with the same base and perpendicular height; see a right triangle as half of a rectangle and any triangle as half of a parallelogram (or as two right triangles); use the resulting formulae A = b × h for parallelograms and A = ½ × b × h for triangles, always using the perpendicular height rather than a slanted side, including when the height falls outside an obtuse triangle; and recognise when an area formula can be used (rectangles, parallelograms, triangles) and when another method is needed, such as counting or estimating squares for an irregular shape
evidence: Cut a right-angled triangle off one end of a parallelogram with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm, move it to the other end to make an 8 cm × 5 cm rectangle, and state the area as 40 cm²

Show that a right triangle with legs 6 cm and 4 cm is half of a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle (12 cm²), and that an obtuse triangle with base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm, drawn outside the triangle, is half of a parallelogram (42 cm²)

Decide that a formula gives the area of a parallelogram with base 10 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm (50 cm², not the 60 cm² from its slanted 6 cm side) but not of an irregular leaf shape, whose area must be estimated by counting squares
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is cutting triangular pieces of cloth where the base is 8 cm and the height is 5 cm, can they use a formula to work out the area of each piece?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Budgets and best buys
topics.description: Solve practical financial problems in Australian dollars and cents — planning a budget, comparing best buys by unit price, and checking reasonableness by estimation — using a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate
evidence: Plan a class party for $60 by choosing items and totalling their costs in a spreadsheet or on a calculator
Decide whether a 2 kg bag of rice for $5.80 or a 500 g bag for $1.60 is better value and explain why
Estimate whether a list of 5 items fits a $25 budget before calculating the exact total
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has $25 to spend on supplies for a school camp, can they plan what to buy, keep a running total, and work out which pack size is better value?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given system (e.g. 5 cm to 0.05 m) using decimal notation to up to three decimal places; convert between smaller and larger units of length, mass, volume, and time
evidence: Convert 3,250 g to 3.25 kg using decimal notation
Convert 0.45 km to 450 m
Explain the relationship between mm, cm, m, and km using powers of 10
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to convert 5 cm to metres and write the answer as a decimal, can they do it — and also convert 2.45 kg into grams?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Measurement Conversions
topics.description: Solve problems involving the calculation and conversion of units of measure, using decimal notation and multi-step reasoning in real-world contexts
evidence: Solve: 'A recipe uses 0.75 kg of flour. How many grams are needed for 3 batches?'
Compare 2.5 litres and 2,450 ml by converting to the same unit
Solve a multi-step problem involving time, distance, and unit conversion
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is filling a fish tank that holds 60 litres and the tap fills it at 3.5 litres per minute, can they work out how long it will take to fill the tank?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Miles & Kilometres
topics.description: Convert between miles and kilometres using the approximate relationship (5 miles ≈ 8 km)
evidence: Convert 40 miles to approximately 64 km
Explain why the conversion factor between miles and km is approximately 1.6
Use the miles↔km relationship to compare a 10 km race with a 6-mile run
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is driving 40 miles to a theme park, can they use the rule that 5 miles ≈ 8 km to estimate roughly how many kilometres that is?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Perimeter (age 10+)
topics.description: Recognise that shapes with the same area can have different perimeters and vice versa; explore this relationship systematically
evidence: Draw two rectangles with area 24 cm² but different perimeters
Find two shapes with perimeter 20 cm but different areas
Explain why a long thin rectangle and a square can have the same area but different perimeters
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 12 square tiles to arrange, can they make different-shaped rectangles and notice that the area stays the same (12 tiles) but the perimeters are all different?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume as additive
topics.description: Recognise volume as additive; find volumes of composite solid figures made of two or more non-overlapping right rectangular prisms
evidence: Decompose an L-shaped solid into two cuboids and calculate total volume
Solve a real-world problem requiring the volume of a composite figure (e.g. a step-shaped structure)
Explain why splitting a composite solid into rectangular prisms allows calculation of total volume
topics.assessmentPrompt: If an L-shaped swimming pool is made of two rectangular sections, can {{name}} find the volume of each section separately and add them to get the total volume of the pool?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume of cuboids
topics.description: Find the volume of right rectangular prisms by packing with unit cubes and show it equals l × w × h (or base area × height); apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h to solve real-world problems; calculate, estimate, and compare volumes of cubes and cuboids in standard units (cm³, m³); and recognise that the formula applies to cuboids, while an irregular solid built from cubes must be counted or split into cuboids
evidence: Use V = l × w × h to find the volume of a cuboid 4 cm × 3 cm × 5 cm = 60 cm³
Explain why packing a prism with unit cubes gives the same result as multiplying edge lengths
Compare the 60 cm³ cuboid with an irregular model built from 58 centimetre cubes, explaining that the formula works for the cuboid but the model's cubes must be counted
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to work out how much soil fits in a plant box that is 40 cm long, 20 cm wide, and 15 cm deep, can they use a formula to calculate the volume?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Area by splitting shapes
topics.description: Find the area of polygons such as trapezoids, kites, rhombuses, irregular quadrilaterals and other rectilinear or non-rectilinear polygons by decomposition or composition: decompose the shape into rectangles and triangles and add the parts, or compose it into an enclosing rectangle and subtract the pieces outside; record the dimensions used for each piece, check that the pieces neither overlap nor leave gaps, and apply this to real-world problems such as floor plans, gardens and signs, giving answers in square units. The focus is the decomposition and composition strategy, which works for any polygon whether or not a dedicated formula is known
evidence: Find the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm by splitting it into a 6 cm × 4 cm rectangle and two triangles with a combined base of 4 cm (24 + 8 = 32 cm²)
Find the area of a kite with diagonals 8 cm and 6 cm by enclosing it in an 8 cm × 6 cm rectangle and subtracting the four corner triangles (48 − 24 = 24 cm²)
Work out the turf needed for a garden shaped like a 12 m × 8 m rectangle with a right triangle (legs 8 m and 3 m) attached to one end (96 + 12 = 108 m²)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a plan of a garden shaped like a rectangle with a triangle on one end, could they split it into the rectangle and the triangle, work out each area and add them to find how much turf to buy?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Discounts, GST and balances
topics.description: Solve and estimate financial problems in Australian dollars involving percentage discounts, adding the 10% GST to prices given before GST (recognising that GST-inclusive prices already contain it), and account balances that go below zero
evidence: Work out the sale price of an $80 jacket with a 25% discount and estimate it first as about $60
For a $45 price given before GST, find the 10% GST of $4.50 and the GST-inclusive price of $49.50, and explain why a price already marked 'GST inclusive' does not get another 10% added
Show a bank balance of $20 that drops by $35 as -$15 on a number line and explain what it means
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees an $80 jacket marked 25% off, can they work out the sale price — and for a $45 price shown before GST, work out what you'd pay once the 10% GST is added?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Spreadsheets for money problems
topics.description: Use a spreadsheet or calculator where appropriate to solve financial problems with decimals and percentages — totalling decimal amounts, applying percentage discounts, and adding 10% GST to prices given before GST — checking results by estimation and justifying the choice of tool
evidence: Build a spreadsheet budget that adds and subtracts amounts such as $12.85, $7.60 and $3.95 and check the running total by rounding
Use a spreadsheet formula to apply a 15% discount to a list of prices and check one result by estimating 15% of $64.90 as about $10
Use a formula to add 10% GST to prices given before GST, and explain why 10% is not added again to a price already marked 'GST inclusive'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Could {{name}} set up a simple spreadsheet for a class fundraiser that totals the costs, takes 15% off sale items, and checks the totals with a quick estimate?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Surface area using nets
topics.description: Represent right rectangular prisms, triangular prisms and pyramids with rectangular or triangular bases using nets made of rectangles and triangles; use the solid's dimensions to label every face on the net; find the surface area as the sum of the face areas, in square units; distinguish surface area (the area covering the outside) from volume (the space inside); and apply this to real-world problems such as wrapping, painting or making boxes, including deciding which faces to include (e.g. an open-topped box)
evidence: Draw the net of a 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm cuboid, label each rectangle's dimensions, and find the surface area as 2 × (20 + 15 + 12) = 94 cm²
Use the net of a square-based pyramid with 6 cm base edges and triangular faces of height 5 cm to find its surface area (36 + 4 × 15 = 96 cm²)
Find the card needed for an open-topped box 30 cm × 20 cm × 10 cm, leaving out the top (600 + 2 × 300 + 2 × 200 = 1,600 cm²), and explain why the answer is in cm² rather than cm³
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} wants to wrap a shoebox 30 cm long, 20 cm wide and 10 cm tall, could they sketch the box unfolded flat, work out the area of each rectangle and add them up to find how much paper is needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Volume with fraction lengths
topics.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths by packing it with cubes whose edge is a suitable unit fraction of a unit (e.g. 1/2 or 1/4), working out the volume of one such cube (a cube with 1/2-unit edges has volume 1/8 cubic unit), counting the cubes and multiplying; show that this gives the same result as multiplying the edge lengths; and apply V = l × w × h and V = B × h with fractional or mixed-number edge lengths in real-world and mathematical problems
evidence: Show that 8 cubes with 1/2 cm edges fit exactly into a 1 cm cube, so each has a volume of 1/8 cm³
Pack a 1½ cm × 1 cm × 2½ cm prism with 1/2 cm cubes (3 × 2 × 5 = 30 cubes), find its volume as 30 × 1/8 = 3¾ cm³, and check that 1½ × 1 × 2½ gives the same answer
Find how much sand fills a box 2¼ ft long, 1½ ft wide and 2/3 ft deep using V = l × w × h (2¼ ft³)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has a gift box 2½ inches long, 1½ inches wide and 2 inches tall, could they work out its volume — and show why filling it with little half-inch cubes gives the same answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as equal sharing
topics.description: Understand division as sharing equally into groups or as grouping (how many groups of a given size can be made)
evidence: Share 10 counters equally between 2 plates
Group 12 objects into sets of 3 and count 4 groups
Use concrete objects to solve 'How many groups of 2 in 8?'
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} has 12 grapes to share equally between 3 friends, can they work out that each friend gets 4 — and explain what they did?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication
topics.description: Use arrays to represent multiplication and division situations
evidence: Build an array of 3 rows of 4 objects to show 3 × 4
Read an array and state the total
Use an array to solve a simple division problem (e.g. 12 objects in rows of 4 → 3 rows)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees eggs arranged in 3 rows of 4 in a box, can they use that grid layout to work out both '3 × 4 = 12' and '12 ÷ 3 = 4'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition
topics.description: Understand multiplication as repeated addition and grouping equal sets
evidence: Explain that 3 groups of 2 is the same as 2 + 2 + 2
Use objects to make equal groups and count the total
Recognise an array as showing equal rows
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to count 4 bags with 3 apples in each, can they see that instead of counting all 12 one by one, they could add 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 — or say '4 groups of 3'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Commutative Multiplication
topics.description: Understand and apply the commutative property of multiplication and recognise that division is not commutative
evidence: Explain that 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 and show this with an array rotated
Use commutativity to choose the easier calculation
Demonstrate that 12 ÷ 3 ≠ 3 ÷ 12
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that 4 × 7 gives the same answer as 7 × 4 — so they can choose whichever order is easier to remember from their times tables?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication as repeated addition (age 6+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using arrays, repeated addition, mental methods, and known facts
evidence: Solve 'There are 5 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples?' using repeated addition or known fact
Solve 'Share 15 sweets equally among 3 children' using grouping
Draw an array to solve a multiplication problem in context
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} 'you have 5 bags with 4 marbles in each — how many altogether?', can they figure it out using objects, a drawing, or mental adding?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd and even numbers
topics.description: Recognise odd and even numbers
evidence: Identify whether a given number is odd or even
Explain that even numbers can be divided into 2 equal groups
Spot the pattern: even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you give {{name}} a number like 37 or 84, can they quickly tell you whether it's odd or even — and explain how they know?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Reading ×, ÷, and = Symbols
topics.description: Read, write, and interpret the symbols ×, ÷, and = in multiplication and division number sentences
evidence: Read 3 × 4 = 12 aloud as 'three times four equals twelve'
Write a multiplication sentence to match an array
Read 12 ÷ 3 = 4 aloud correctly
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you write '6 × 4 = 24' or '15 ÷ 3 = 5' on paper, can {{name}} tell you what the times sign, division sign, and equals sign each mean?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sharing and grouping problems
topics.description: Model practical equal-sharing and grouping problems up to about 30 with diagrams, physical objects and virtual materials (dragging on-screen objects into equal groups or arrays), and solve them using skip counting or repeated addition
evidence: Solve 'share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends' by dragging on-screen stickers into 3 groups and say each friend gets 6
Solve 'how many bags of 5 apples can we make from 20?' with real apples or counters and skip count the bags
Draw a diagram of 4 tables with 4 chairs each and check the total of 16 with an on-screen array
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to share 18 stickers equally among 3 friends, can they work it out by sorting them into groups — either with the real stickers or on a tablet?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 2, 5, and 10 multiplication tables
evidence: Quickly answer 5 × 3 = 15 from memory
Quickly answer 20 ÷ 5 = 4 from memory
Recite the 2, 5, and 10 times tables fluently
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall times table facts from the 2s, 5s, and 10s — like '5 × 6 = 30' or '20 ÷ 2 = 10' — forwards and backwards?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Arrays for multiplication (age 7+)
topics.description: Use addition to find the total number of objects arranged in rectangular arrays with up to 5 rows and 5 columns; write an equation to express the total as a sum of equal addends
evidence: Count objects in a 3×4 array and write 4 + 4 + 4 = 12
Explain that each row has the same number of objects so the total can be found by repeated addition
Draw a rectangular array to model a given repeated-addition equation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees 4 rows of 5 stickers on a sheet, can they use repeated addition — '5 + 5 + 5 + 5' — to find the total, and write it as an equation?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-Step Multiply & Divide
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division, including scaling problems and correspondence problems where n objects are connected to m objects
evidence: Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'the ribbon is 3 times as long')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '4 shirts and 3 trousers — how many outfits?')
Solve a missing-number multiplication or division problem
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe for 4 people needs 3 eggs, can {{name}} work out how many eggs are needed for 8 people — recognising it as a doubling or scaling problem?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rows & Columns in Rectangles
topics.description: Partition a rectangle into rows and columns of same-size squares and count to find the total number of them
evidence: Divide a rectangle into equal rows and columns of unit squares
Count the total number of squares using repeated addition or skip counting
Relate the rows-and-columns structure to a rectangular array
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} draw lines to divide a rectangle into a neat grid of equal squares, then count all the squares to find the total?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Times tables (age 7+)
topics.description: Recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4, and 8 multiplication tables
evidence: Recall 3 × 1 through 3 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 4 × 1 through 4 × 12 and corresponding division facts
Recall 8 × 1 through 8 × 12 and corresponding division facts
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly recall facts from the 3, 4, and 8 times tables — like '8 × 7 = 56' or '36 ÷ 4 = 9' — without having to work them out each time?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Written Multiplication & Division
topics.description: Write and calculate mathematical statements for multiplication and division using known tables, including two-digit × one-digit, using mental and progressing to formal written methods
evidence: Calculate 23 × 4 using partitioning (20 × 4 + 3 × 4)
Calculate 96 ÷ 8 using known table facts
Begin to use a formal written layout for short multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out sums like '23 × 4' or '68 ÷ 4' — either in their head using times table knowledge, or by writing it out step by step?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: All times tables to 12×12
topics.description: Recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12
evidence: Recall any fact from the 1–12 times tables rapidly
Recall the corresponding division fact for any multiplication fact
Use known facts to check or derive answers in calculations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} recall any multiplication or division fact from all the times tables up to 12 — like '9 × 8 = 72' or '132 ÷ 12 = 11' — quickly and accurately?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division as Unknown Factor
topics.description: Understand division as an unknown-factor problem (e.g. find 32 ÷ 8 by finding the number that makes 32 when multiplied by 8)
evidence: Explain that 32 ÷ 8 = ? is the same as 8 × ? = 32
Use a known multiplication fact to find a division answer
Describe the relationship between multiplication and division as inverse operations
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '32 ÷ 8' by asking 'what do I multiply 8 by to get 32?' — using times table knowledge rather than a separate division method?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factor Pairs & Commutativity
topics.description: Recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations
evidence: List all factor pairs of a given number (e.g. 24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6)
Use commutativity to reorder a multiplication for easier mental calculation
Explain what a factor pair is and how commutativity helps
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to multiply '4 × 15', can they spot that splitting it into '4 × 5 × 3 = 20 × 3 = 60' is a clever shortcut — using factor pairs to make it easier?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Fluent multiplication and division facts
topics.description: Fluently multiply and divide within 100 using strategies such as the relationship between multiplication and division
evidence: Answer any single-digit multiplication fact within 3 seconds
Answer any related division fact within 3 seconds
Use known facts to derive unknown facts (e.g. 9 × 7 from 10 × 7 − 7)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} answer any times table fact up to 10 × 10 quickly — and also give the related division facts, like '63 ÷ 9 = 7' from knowing '9 × 7 = 63'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental multiplication and division
topics.description: Use place value, known and derived facts to multiply and divide mentally, including multiplying by 0 and 1, dividing by 1, and multiplying together three numbers
evidence: Calculate 40 × 6 = 240 mentally using place value
Explain why any number × 0 = 0 and any number × 1 = the number itself
Multiply three numbers mentally by choosing a useful pair first (e.g. 2 × 7 × 5 = 2 × 5 × 7 = 70)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out things like '6 × 0', '1 × 35', or '100 ÷ 100' instantly in their head — using what they know rather than working everything out from scratch?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplication and Division Word Problems
topics.description: Use multiplication and division within 100 to solve word problems involving equal groups, arrays, and measurement quantities
evidence: Solve an equal-groups word problem using multiplication
Solve a measurement division problem (e.g. 'How many 4-cm pieces from a 28-cm ribbon?')
Solve an array/area word problem using multiplication
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you tell {{name}} 'there are 7 boxes with 9 pencils in each — how many pencils?', can they recognise it as a multiplication problem and solve it correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiply & Add Problems
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplying and adding, including using the distributive law, integer scaling problems, and harder correspondence problems
evidence: Use the distributive law to solve 14 × 6 as 10 × 6 + 4 × 6
Solve a scaling problem (e.g. 'A tower is 3 times as tall as a 15 m building')
Solve a correspondence problem (e.g. '3 types of bread, 4 types of filling — how many different sandwiches?')
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} needs to work out '5 × 23', can they split it into '5 × 20 + 5 × 3 = 100 + 15 = 115' — rather than just jumping straight to a written method?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying by Tens
topics.description: Multiply one-digit whole numbers by multiples of 10 in the range 10–90 using strategies based on place value and properties of operations
evidence: Calculate 7 × 30 = 210 by reasoning 7 × 3 tens = 21 tens = 210
Explain why multiplying by a multiple of 10 adds a zero to the product
Use this skill to estimate products of larger numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '7 × 40' or '6 × 80' by first doing the single-digit multiplication and then placing the zero — getting 280 and 480?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Patterns in Times Tables
topics.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table) and explain them using properties of operations
evidence: Notice that all products of 5 end in 0 or 5 and explain why
Observe that the sum of two even numbers is always even
Identify a pattern in the multiplication table and explain it using commutativity or the distributive property
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} spot patterns in times tables — like all multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5 — and explain why that pattern happens?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Properties of Operations
topics.description: Apply properties of operations (commutative, associative, distributive) as strategies to multiply and divide
evidence: Use commutativity: if 6 × 4 = 24 then 4 × 6 = 24
Use the distributive property: 8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 = 40 + 16 = 56
Use associativity to multiply three numbers: 2 × 3 × 5 = 6 × 5 = 30
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use tricks like breaking up a number — working out '6 × 14' as '6 × 10 + 6 × 4 = 60 + 24 = 84' — to make multiplication easier?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Unknown in Multiplication & Division
topics.description: Determine the unknown whole number in a multiplication or division equation relating three whole numbers (e.g. 8 × ? = 48, ? × 6 = 42)
evidence: Find the missing factor in 7 × ? = 63
Find the missing dividend in ? ÷ 5 = 9
Explain the strategy used (e.g. using the related multiplication fact)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '8 × ? = 48' or '? ÷ 6 = 7' written on paper, can they figure out what number goes in the blank?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Division Means
topics.description: Interpret whole-number quotients (e.g. 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share or the number of equal groups)
evidence: Explain that 56 ÷ 8 can mean sharing 56 into 8 equal groups or making groups of 8
Draw a picture to represent a division expression
Match a division expression to a word problem involving equal sharing or grouping
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} explain that '56 ÷ 8' could mean 'if 56 things are shared between 8 people, how many does each person get?' — not just recite the answer '7'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: What Multiplication Means
topics.description: Interpret products of whole numbers (e.g. 5 × 7 as the total number of objects in 5 groups of 7)
evidence: Explain that 4 × 6 means 4 groups of 6 objects
Draw a picture or array to represent a multiplication expression
Match a multiplication expression to a word problem involving equal groups
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '5 × 7' written down, can they explain it means 5 groups with 7 in each group — not just recite the answer '35'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Written Multiplication
topics.description: Multiply two-digit and three-digit numbers by a one-digit number using formal written layout
evidence: Set out and solve 47 × 6 using short multiplication
Set out and solve 234 × 5 using short multiplication with carrying
Check the answer using estimation (e.g. 234 × 5 ≈ 200 × 5 = 1000)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '347 × 6' by setting it out formally in a column — multiplying each digit separately and carrying where needed?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with remainders
topics.description: Solve multi-step word problems using the four operations with whole numbers, including interpreting remainders in context; represent with equations using a letter for the unknown; check with estimation
evidence: 52 children go on a trip in minibuses holding 9 each — how many minibuses are needed? (interpret remainder)
A shop sells packs of 6 pencils for £1.50 each — how much do 5 packs cost?
Represent a two-step problem with an equation using n for the unknown
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} reads 'a school buys 7 boxes of 24 pens and shares them equally between 8 classes', can they work through all the steps and decide sensibly what to do with any remainder?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes
topics.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100; identify common factors and common multiples of two numbers; use these concepts to solve problems
evidence: State the first five multiples of 7
Find the common factors of 24 and 36
Find all common factors of 36 and 48
Identify the first three common multiples of 6 and 8
Determine whether a given number (e.g. 97) is prime and justify the reasoning
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} list all the factor pairs for a number like 36 — (1, 36), (2, 18), (3, 12), (4, 9), (6, 6) — and find factors that two numbers share?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes (age 9+)
topics.description: Solve problems involving multiplication and division using knowledge of factors, multiples, squares, and cubes
evidence: Is 156 a multiple of 6? Explain how you know
Find two square numbers that add to make 100
Use factor pairs to simplify 24 × 25 as 6 × (4 × 25) = 6 × 100 = 600
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is asked to find all the square numbers less than 100, can they work through it systematically and give you the correct list: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Long multiplication
topics.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using formal written methods including long multiplication; illustrate with area models
evidence: Calculate 2,347 × 6 using formal written layout
Calculate 34 × 27 using long multiplication
Draw an area model for 45 × 23 and connect to the written method
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out something like '2,346 × 7' or '43 × 28' using the formal column method — setting it out carefully and working through all the steps?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental multiplication and division (age 9+)
topics.description: Multiply and divide numbers mentally drawing upon known facts, including related facts and place-value adjustments
evidence: Calculate 40 × 60 mentally by using 4 × 6 = 24 then appending zeros
Derive 7 × 15 by calculating 7 × 10 + 7 × 5
Calculate 360 ÷ 9 mentally using 36 ÷ 9 = 4
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out things like '24 × 5' or '360 ÷ 8' in their head — using clever connections to known facts rather than needing to write anything down?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplicative Comparison
topics.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison (e.g. 35 = 5 × 7 means 35 is 5 times as many as 7); represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as equations
evidence: Explain that '4 times as many' means multiply by 4
Write an equation for: Sarah has 3 times as many stickers as Tom, who has 8 stickers
Distinguish multiplicative comparison from additive comparison in word problems
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at '35 = 5 × 7' and explain it as '35 is five times as many as 7' — understanding it as a comparison, not just a multiplication fact?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplicative Comparison
topics.description: Solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number
evidence: A blue ribbon is 3 times as long as a red ribbon of 7 cm — how long is the blue ribbon?
36 is 4 times a number — what is the number?
Explain why 'Sam has 5 more' is additive but 'Sam has 5 times as many' is multiplicative
topics.assessmentPrompt: If you say 'Maya has 4 times as many stickers as Tom, and Tom has 6 — how many does Maya have?', can {{name}} recognise this as a multiplication problem and solve it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying and dividing
topics.description: Multiply and divide whole numbers and those involving decimals by 10, 100, and 1000
evidence: Calculate 3.45 × 100 = 345
Calculate 72 ÷ 1000 = 0.072
Explain that multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} quickly work out '4.7 × 100' or '3,600 ÷ 1,000' — knowing that digits shift left or right in the place-value chart depending on whether they're multiplying or dividing?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Odd and even number rules
topics.description: Explain and use the properties of odd and even numbers when adding, subtracting and multiplying, e.g. odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, and any whole number multiplied by an even number is even
evidence: Explain with paired counters why the sum of two odd numbers is always even
Predict without calculating whether 347 + 129 is odd or even and justify it
Explain why 6 x 37 must be even
topics.assessmentPrompt: Without adding them up, can {{name}} tell you whether 347 + 129 will be odd or even — and explain why?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Prime numbers
topics.description: Know and use the vocabulary of prime numbers, prime factors, and composite numbers; establish whether a number up to 100 is prime; recall prime numbers up to 19
evidence: Explain that a prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself
Determine whether 51 is prime or composite and justify the answer
List all prime numbers up to 19 from memory
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} tell you what makes a number 'prime' — that it only divides exactly by 1 and itself — and give some examples like 7, 11, and 13?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Shape patterns
topics.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule; identify apparent features of the pattern not explicit in the rule and explain informally why they occur
evidence: Given 'start at 1, add 3', generate terms and notice they alternate odd/even
Given a shape pattern, predict the next three terms and describe the rule
Explain why starting at 2 and adding 4 always gives even numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is told 'start at 3 and multiply by 2 each time', can they write out the pattern — 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 — and spot any interesting features in how it grows?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Short division with remainders
topics.description: Divide numbers up to four digits by a one-digit number using short division (and place-value/array strategies); interpret remainders appropriately for the context
evidence: Calculate 4,932 ÷ 6 using short division
Solve 125 ÷ 8 and interpret: 15 remainder 5 means 15 full bags with 5 left over
Use the multiplication–division relationship to check a division answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use the short division ('bus stop') method to work out something like '2,457 ÷ 6', and decide what to do with any remainder left over?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Square and cube numbers
topics.description: Recognise and use square numbers and cube numbers, and the notation for squared (²) and cubed (³)
evidence: Identify 49 as 7² and explain that 7 × 7 = 49
Calculate 4³ = 64 and explain it means 4 × 4 × 4
List the first ten square numbers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Does {{name}} know that '5²' means 5 × 5 = 25 and '3³' means 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 — and can they work out other squared and cubed numbers?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Understanding fractions
topics.description: Solve problems involving scaling by simple fractions and problems involving simple rates
evidence: A recipe for 4 people needs 200 g of flour — how much for 6 people?
If 3 kg costs £12, how much does 5 kg cost?
Scale a shape by a factor of 1/2 and find the new dimensions
topics.assessmentPrompt: If a recipe serves 4 and {{name}} wants to make it for 6, can they scale up each ingredient — for example, changing '2 cups of flour' to '3 cups'?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Brackets in Expressions
topics.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions and evaluate expressions containing these grouping symbols
evidence: Evaluate 3 × (4 + 5) by computing inside the parentheses first
Evaluate {2 × [3 + (7 − 1)]} with nested grouping symbols
Insert parentheses into an expression to make it equal a target value
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at '3 × (4 + 5)' and work out the brackets first — getting '3 × 9 = 27' — rather than just multiplying left to right?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Calculators for multiplying and dividing
topics.description: Use a calculator or spreadsheet where appropriate to multiply larger numbers and to divide, check results by estimation, and interpret a decimal calculator answer to a division in context as a whole number, a remainder, a fraction or a decimal
evidence: Use a calculator for 2365 x 48 and check the answer against an estimate of 2000 x 50 = 100 000
Divide 250 by 8 on a calculator, read 31.25, and interpret it as 32 buses needed, 31 full boxes with 2 left over, or 31.25 cm of ribbon each, depending on the problem
Choose a mental strategy for 47 x 10 and a calculator for 3847 x 26, and justify each choice
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} divides 250 by 8 on a calculator and sees 31.25, can they work out what that means for the problem — like needing 32 buses, not 31.25?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Decimal place value
topics.description: Multiply one-digit numbers with up to two decimal places by whole numbers (e.g. 3.47 × 6)
evidence: Correctly compute 4.56 × 7 using a written method
Use place-value reasoning to explain why 3.2 × 5 = 16.0
Model a decimal multiplication using an area diagram or expanded form
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '3.47 × 6' — keeping the decimal point in the right place and carrying correctly through each column?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Dividing by two-digit numbers
topics.description: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit number using formal written short division where appropriate, interpreting remainders according to context
evidence: Use short division to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 efficiently
Explain when short division is more appropriate than long division
Interpret a remainder as a decimal or fraction in a measurement context
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use short division to work out something like '2,184 ÷ 12' — keeping track of each digit and carrying any remainders into the next column?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with Decimals
topics.description: Use written division methods in cases where the answer has up to two decimal places; divide decimals to hundredths by whole numbers
evidence: Compute 14.76 ÷ 4 using a written method to get 3.69
Explain how to continue long division past the decimal point to obtain a decimal quotient
Solve a context problem that requires dividing a decimal amount equally (e.g. sharing £18.60 among 5 people)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use a written method to calculate something like '17 ÷ 4 = 4.25' — carrying the division past the decimal point to get a decimal answer rather than a remainder?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Division with remainders (age 10+)
topics.description: Divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal written long division, interpreting remainders as whole numbers, fractions, or by rounding as appropriate
evidence: Compute 4,752 ÷ 13 using long division and express the remainder as a fraction
Decide whether to round up or down a division remainder in a real-life context (e.g. buses needed)
Explain each step of the long division algorithm for a 4-digit ÷ 2-digit calculation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use long division to work out something like '1,848 ÷ 24' — going through the steps of divide, multiply, subtract, and bring down until they reach the answer?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimation to check answers to calculations
topics.description: Use estimation to check answers to calculations and determine, in the context of a problem, an appropriate degree of accuracy
evidence: Estimate 487 × 23 by rounding to 500 × 20 and use this to check a calculated answer
Determine whether an exact answer or an estimate is more appropriate in a given context
Spot an unreasonable answer by comparing with a quick mental estimate
topics.assessmentPrompt: Before {{name}} works out a large multiplication or division, can they estimate what the answer should be roughly — and then check whether their final answer is in the right ballpark?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factor algorithms and spreadsheets
topics.description: Create and use algorithms with steps and decisions, and digital tools such as spreadsheets, to experiment with factors, multiples and divisibility, and describe the patterns that emerge
evidence: Write an algorithm that tests every number from 1 to 24 and records it if 24 divided by it leaves no remainder
Use a spreadsheet column of multiples of 6 and highlight those that are also multiples of 4
Describe the pattern found when listing numbers between 1 and 50 that have exactly two factors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} set up a list or spreadsheet to find all the numbers that divide into 24 — and spot patterns, like which numbers have only two factors?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Long multiplication (age 10+)
topics.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers (up to 4 digits by 2 digits) using the formal written method of long multiplication
evidence: Correctly compute 2,463 × 37 using long multiplication
Explain each partial product in a long multiplication and why they are added
Multiply a four-digit number by a two-digit number without procedural errors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} use long multiplication to work out something like '2,347 × 24' — setting it out in two rows, one for the units and one for the tens, then adding the results?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Mental calculation strategies
topics.description: Perform mental calculations including with mixed operations and large numbers, using strategies such as partitioning, compensation, and derived facts
evidence: Mentally compute 45 × 8 by partitioning into 40 × 8 + 5 × 8
Use known facts to derive 6.5 × 4 mentally
Solve a multi-operation mental calculation such as 250 × 3 + 500 and explain the strategy used
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out a mixed calculation like '(200 × 6) + 350 − 75' entirely in their head — keeping track of each step without writing anything down?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multiplying and dividing (age 10+)
topics.description: Multiply and divide numbers by 10, 100, and 1000 giving answers up to three decimal places, understanding that digits shift position in the place-value chart
evidence: Compute 3.456 × 100 = 345.6 correctly
Compute 45.2 ÷ 1000 = 0.0452 correctly
Explain why multiplying by 10 shifts each digit one place to the left
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} work out '4.6 ÷ 1,000 = 0.0046' — knowing that each division by 10 shifts digits one place to the right, even past the decimal point?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Multi-step problems: choosing operations
topics.description: Solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, deciding which operations and methods to use and why; solve multi-step problems in contexts
evidence: Solve a three-step word problem involving a mix of all four operations
Explain why particular operations were chosen for each step of a multi-step problem
Identify and correct an error in a multi-step solution that used the wrong operation
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} is given a multi-step problem mixing different operations — like working out the total cost of several items at different prices — can they plan and carry out each step correctly?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Order of operations
topics.description: Understand and apply the conventional order of operations (PEMDAS/BODMAS) to carry out calculations involving the four operations
evidence: Explain why 8 + 2 × 5 = 18 (not 50) by referencing multiplication before addition
Evaluate a multi-step expression like 12 ÷ 3 + 4 × 2 correctly as 12
State the correct order: brackets, then orders/exponents, then multiplication/division (L→R), then addition/subtraction (L→R)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} sees '8 + 4 × 3', do they get 20 — not 36 — because they know to do the multiplication before the addition?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Rounding Answers
topics.description: Solve problems which require answers to be rounded to specified degrees of accuracy
evidence: Compute a division and round the result to one decimal place as specified
Determine the appropriate degree of accuracy for a measurement context (e.g. round to nearest penny)
Solve a problem where an unrounded decimal answer must be interpreted in context (e.g. whole containers needed)
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} calculates an answer of 8.63 but the question asks for it to the nearest whole number, can they round it correctly to 9 — and explain why that level of precision matters in context?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Writing Number Sentences
topics.description: Write simple numerical expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them (e.g. recognise that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921)
evidence: Write an expression for 'add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2' using parentheses
Explain what 4 × (365 − 12) represents without computing it
Compare two expressions and determine which is larger without evaluating
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} look at '4 × (5 + 3)' and say 'that's 4 times the result of adding 5 and 3' — reading the expression as a description of a calculation, without having to work it out first?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Estimating to check decimals
topics.description: Use estimation and rounding to check the reasonableness of answers when multiplying and dividing decimals (including by multiples of powers of 10), identifying misplaced decimal points
evidence: Estimate 4.87 x 30 as about 5 x 30 = 150 before calculating 146.1
Decide whether 63.6 / 20 = 31.8 is reasonable by rounding to 60 / 20 = 3 and find the error
Round 2.46 x 400 to 2.5 x 400 = 1000 to check a calculated answer of 984
topics.assessmentPrompt: If {{name}} works out 4.87 x 30 and gets 1461, do they notice it can't be right because 5 x 30 is only about 150?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Factors, multiples, and primes (age 11+)
topics.description: Use the concepts and vocabulary of prime numbers, factors, multiples, common factors, common multiples, highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and prime factorisation including product notation and the unique factorisation property
evidence: Express any integer as a product of its prime factors using index notation
Find the HCF and LCM of two numbers using prime factorisation
Apply the unique factorisation theorem to explain why every number has exactly one set of prime factors
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} find the highest common factor of two numbers like 24 and 36 — working out the biggest number that divides exactly into both — and explain how they found it?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Priority of operations
topics.description: Use conventional notation for the priority of operations including brackets, powers, roots, and reciprocals; apply BIDMAS/BODMAS consistently to evaluate complex numerical expressions
evidence: Evaluate expressions involving brackets, indices, and all four operations in the correct order
Explain why the order of operations is necessary to avoid ambiguity
Use the reciprocal of a number and understand that a number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1
topics.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} evaluate a complex expression like '5 + 2³ ÷ 4' correctly — applying the right order of operations, handling the power before the division and division before the addition?

topics.subject: Mathematics
topics.name: Sign Rules for Multiplication
topics.description: Multiply and divide with positive and negative integers and rational numbers, understanding the rules for the sign of the product or quotient
evidence: Apply the sign rules when multiplying two integers (positive × negative, negative × negative)
